meta.blurb: An old man falls asleep at Corin's ferry and does not wake, leaving a glowing lantern in the boy's hands. Outside, a grey fog wipes out the memory of everyone it touches. Corin must carry the light to the Beacon at Cairnhead.
meta.bible: Corin Thatch: fifteen-year-old ferryman's son from Saltreach, quiet, stubborn and brave; the Lantern-bearer. Juniper: Corin's brown ferry dog, loyal and clever. Brother Aldous Wick: the old Keeper of the Tower at Aldermoor, who gives Corin the Dawnlight before he dies. Mara Thatch: Corin's mother, who mends nets. Rook Tarn: a witty barge-woman with a river barge called the Kestrel; she knows rivers, harbours and the sea. Dame Isaura Brack: a retired mountain guide with a bad knee, gruff and wise. Pell Ainsley: a young scribe from Millbrook who never forgets anything; he carries a book called the Long Memory. Marigold Fenn: a beekeeper who lives in the Thornwood. Keeper Ansel Dray: once the Keeper of the Beacon at Cairnhead; now the Pale Regent, a tall figure of fog who wears a Keeper's chain. Aldermoor: the land, and also the name of the Tower where the last lantern was kept. The Dawnlight: the last lantern, which burns with a flame that never goes out by itself. The Grey: a creeping fog that makes people forget their names, their homes and the people they love; it is not a weapon, it is a sadness that spreads. The Hushed: people already taken by the Grey, who walk silently and follow it. The Beacons: seven great fires, once lit across Aldermoor from the tower on Cairnhead, now all dark but the Dawnlight. Saltreach: Corin's marsh village on the River Wendle. Millbrook: the river town where Pell lives. The Long Road: the old road across the country. Thornwood: the old forest. Hightarn Pass: the snowy mountain pass. The Salt Flats: a vast white plain that shines like a mirror. Port Larrow: the harbour town with a dark lighthouse. Cairnhead: the sea cliff where the first and greatest Beacon stands. Davin Thatch: Corin's father, the old ferryman, who died of a winter fever when Corin was seven. Tobias Reed: the old fisherman of Saltreach, the first person there to forget. Granny Wenna: the oldest woman in Saltreach, who tells the old tale of the seven Beacons. Nan Pruitt: Saltreach's healer. Wilf Gorse: Saltreach's carpenter. Hob Garrick: a kindly farmer with a cart and a grey mare called Dumpling. Pip Cobb: a nine-year-old Millbrook boy, taken by the Grey and woken by Pell's reading. Orla Finch: the head librarian of Millbrook, Pell's teacher. Dunstan Tarn: Rook's cousin, who minds the Kestrel at Millbrook. Bess Harker: the innkeeper of the Wheatsheaf on the Long Road. Tam Brack: Isaura's late husband, a shepherd and guide. Bramble: Isaura's old sheepdog. Ironcrown: the highest peak of the Hightarn Pass. Osric Vane: the keeper of the Port Larrow lighthouse, one of the Hushed. Tilda Vane: Osric's daughter, a sailmaker, who gives the travellers the Heron. The Heron: a small sailing boat with a patched grey sail. The Fisher's Rest: the harbour inn at Port Larrow. Lena and Wren: Ansel Dray's wife and daughter, lost to a winter sickness. The seven Beacons stood at Cairnhead, Hightarn, Longmere, Thornhill, Millhill, Larrowhead and Marshend. The Tower of Aldermoor: an old stone tower on the hills two days' walk upriver from Saltreach, where Aldous kept the Dawnlight for forty years. The Wendle: the slow river that runs past Saltreach to Millbrook. Mara gives Corin her net-mending needle and a coil of cord. Rules of the Dawnlight: its flame leans toward the right path and grows brighter with every true story told beside it. Nobody dies in battle in this book. Voice and tone: an old-fashioned adventure told warmly and clearly; danger is real but no one is killed in battle; the Grey is beaten by memory, kindness and shared stories rather than by swords.
chapters: The Gift on the Far Bank

beats.scene: Corin poles a flat ferry across a misty marsh river at dawn
beats.summary: Corin Thatch, a ferryman's son, poles the ferry across the Wendle at dawn in the marsh village of Saltreach.

beats.scene: A brown dog sits at the front of a flat ferry
beats.summary: Juniper rides the ferry every day and knows every passenger by smell.

beats.scene: A woman mends a fishing net by a cottage window at dusk
beats.summary: At home Corin's mother Mara mends nets, and they remember Corin's father, who died when Corin was small.

beats.scene: Villagers wait on a wooden landing with baskets and sacks
beats.summary: The regular passengers, among them old Tobias, show how much the village depends on the ferry and on Corin's quiet kindness.

beats.scene: Traders at a market stall talk gravely as villagers listen
beats.summary: On market day, travelling traders bring news of a grey fog that has swallowed towns in the east.

beats.scene: An old woman tells children a story beside a marsh fire
beats.summary: Granny Wenna tells the old tale of the seven Beacons, and the children think it is only a story.

beats.scene: Marsh birds rise silent into the sky above grey reeds
beats.summary: At dusk the marsh birds fall silent and a long grey bank appears on the horizon.

beats.scene: Villagers stand on the landing watching a grey wall on the horizon
beats.summary: The village gathers to watch the fog creep closer, and the bell is rung.

beats.scene: A boy and dog sit awake at a window as fog creeps by
beats.summary: At night the fog slides through the lanes of Saltreach, cold and silent.

beats.scene: An old fisherman stands in front of his own door, bewildered
beats.summary: In the morning old Tobias stands before his own house, unable to remember his name.

beats.scene: Villagers gather around a confused old fisherman in a muddy lane
beats.summary: The village crowds around Tobias, and the healer Nan Pruitt finds no fever and no wound.

beats.scene: A boy kneels before a blank-faced old man and speaks to him
beats.summary: Corin tries to tell Tobias his own name without success, and more people in the lane are touched by the Grey.

beats.scene: Villagers argue around a table in a lamplit hall
beats.summary: The village meets to decide whether to flee, and Mara says every window must keep a lamp burning.

beats.scene: A boy and a dog walk to a lonely ferry landing at night
beats.summary: Late that night Corin goes to check the ferry's ropes, and Juniper whines at the dark river.

beats.scene: A wounded old man in a torn cloak steps onto Corin's night ferry
beats.summary: An old man in a torn grey cloak staggers out of the fog and begs a crossing, with a faint golden light beneath his coat.

beats.scene: A ferry crosses a black river with golden light spreading around it
beats.summary: Corin poles across the river while the fog draws back from the glow, and the old man gives his name as Brother Aldous Wick.

beats.scene: An old man opens his cloak to reveal a glowing lantern on a ferry
beats.summary: In midstream Aldous reveals the Dawnlight, the last lantern in Aldermoor.

beats.scene: Seven fires burn on distant hills in an old painted scene
beats.summary: Aldous tells how the seven Beacons went dark one by one and the Grey crept farther each year.

beats.scene: An old man glances anxiously at grey shapes on the river bank
beats.summary: Aldous warns that the Grey hunts the Dawnlight, the one flame that will not go out by itself, and the Hushed follow it.

beats.scene: Brother Aldous points to a distant sea cliff on an old map
beats.summary: Aldous shows on a map that the Dawnlight must be carried to Cairnhead, where the first and greatest Beacon stands.

beats.scene: A ferry bumps the far river bank under a weeping willow
beats.summary: On the far bank Aldous, too weak to go on, sits against an old willow, and Corin makes him comfortable.

beats.scene: An old man gestures toward distant hills as a lantern glows
beats.summary: Aldous tells of the Tower of Aldermoor, where he kept the Dawnlight for forty years until the Grey came close.

beats.scene: A lantern's flame leans toward a boy's outstretched hand
beats.summary: Aldous holds out the lantern and its flame leans toward Corin, while Juniper wags her tail.

beats.scene: A boy shakes his head, holding up his empty hands
beats.summary: Corin refuses, saying he is only a ferryman's son and that someone braver should go.

beats.scene: An old man smiles at a boy beside a glowing lantern
beats.summary: Aldous answers that a river is crossed one push of the pole at a time, and the light needs a friend, not a hero.

beats.scene: An old man presses a brass lantern into a boy's hands
beats.summary: Corin accepts the Dawnlight, and Aldous gives him two rules for keeping it.

beats.scene: An old man sleeps beneath a willow while a boy and dog keep watch
beats.summary: Aldous falls into a deep sleep from which he does not wake.

beats.scene: Villagers carry a wrapped figure up a grassy slope at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Corin and a few villagers bury Aldous beneath the willow and mark the place with a stone.

beats.scene: A woman looks at a glowing lantern on a kitchen table
beats.summary: Corin tells his mother everything, and the golden light moves across her tired face.

beats.scene: A woman and her son sit at a table with a lantern between them
beats.summary: Mara says that the fog will reach their door too and that someone must carry the light to the sea.

beats.scene: A woman packs bread and wool socks into a worn leather bag
beats.summary: Mara packs bread, cheese, dried apples and warm socks through the night.

beats.scene: A woman presses a bone needle and coiled cord into a boy's hand
beats.summary: Before dawn Mara gives Corin her net-mending needle and a coil of strong cord.

beats.scene: Villagers gather in a muddy lane with lamps to wave goodbye
beats.summary: Villagers who still remember themselves gather to see Corin off, and Nan Pruitt gives him a pot of salve.

beats.scene: A woman kisses her son goodbye in a doorway as fog gathers behind them
beats.summary: Mara kisses Corin goodbye at the cottage door while the fog gathers at the end of the lane.

beats.scene: A boy and a dog follow a river bank path away from a village
beats.summary: Corin and Juniper leave Saltreach along the river path.

beats.scene: A boy looks back at a distant village sinking into grey fog
beats.summary: Corin looks back once, then lifts the lantern and sees the fog on the path draw back from it.

beats.scene: A boy sleeps beneath a hawthorn tree beside a glowing lantern
beats.summary: On the first night Corin makes camp under a hawthorn, and Juniper keeps him company.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf waves from a river barge
beats.summary: In the morning Corin meets Rook Tarn, a bold barge-woman, on the river.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf laughs on a barge deck beside a boy
beats.summary: Rook jokes with Corin and says river people never charge each other for a ride.

beats.scene: A barge slips its mooring rope and glides into the current
beats.summary: Rook agrees to carry Corin down to Millbrook, and the Kestrel casts off.

beats.scene: A barge glides downriver as lantern light pushes back the fog
beats.summary: The Grey follows the barge along the bank, and the Dawnlight pushes it back like a wall.

beats.scene: A boy learns to steer a barge tiller beside a woman
beats.summary: Rook lets Corin take the tiller on the long straight stretches, and he learns quickly.

beats.scene: A woman tells a story on a barge deck beside a lantern at night
beats.summary: After dark Rook tells Corin how the Beacons were first lit.

beats.scene: A woman counts seven fires on her fingers beside a map of valleys
beats.summary: Rook names the seven Beacons and the valleys they watched over.

beats.scene: A woman sits at the stern of a barge looking at the stars
beats.summary: Rook admits she once crewed a seagoing ship and left the sea after a great storm.

beats.scene: Silent villagers stand along a river bank watching a passing barge
beats.summary: The Kestrel passes a riverside village where silent people turn to watch it go by.

beats.scene: A barge anchored in the middle of a dark river under stars
beats.summary: Rook anchors in midstream for the night and takes the first watch.

beats.scene: A boy dreams of an old man beneath a willow as a lantern flickers
beats.summary: Corin dreams of Aldous, and wakes to find the flame shivering.

beats.scene: Smoke rises from mill chimneys above stone bridges at sunrise
beats.summary: At sunrise the chimneys and mill wheels of Millbrook come into view.

beats.scene: A barge ties up at a stone quay in a busy market town
beats.summary: The Kestrel reaches Millbrook, where many people already move slowly and absently under the Grey.

beats.scene: A busy market square with stalls of wool, apples and rope
beats.summary: Corin follows Rook into the great market of Millbrook and is dizzy with the crowd.

beats.scene: A baker stares at her own loaves, unsure of the price
beats.summary: A baker forgets the price of her bread and the town crier reads the same notice three times.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf points at distant white mountains
beats.summary: Rook points to the far mountains and says they need a guide who knows snow.

beats.scene: A tall weathered woman with a walking stick studies a map on a stall
beats.summary: In the market Corin meets Dame Isaura Brack, who guided travellers over the mountains for thirty years.

beats.scene: A tall woman folds her arms and shakes her head at a boy
beats.summary: Isaura refuses, saying she is retired and her knee is bad.

beats.scene: A cloaked thief grabs at a lantern in a crowded market as people scatter
beats.summary: A thief in a dark cloak snatches at the Dawnlight, and Corin holds on.

beats.scene: A young scribe swings a thick leather book at a fallen thief
beats.summary: A young man swings a heavy book and knocks the thief down.

beats.scene: A thief runs between market stalls as a walking stick trips him
beats.summary: The thief flees, shouting that a grey voice promised him bread for the light.

beats.scene: A thin young scribe with ink-stained fingers holds a thick leather book
beats.summary: The scribe is Pell Ainsley, who remembers everything he reads and keeps a book called the Long Memory.

beats.scene: Four travellers and a dog stand together beside a glowing lantern
beats.summary: Pell asks to join them, Isaura agrees, and she notices that her knee has stopped hurting.

beats.scene: A woman hands a mooring rope to her cousin on a river dock
beats.summary: Rook leaves the Kestrel with her cousin Dunstan, and the four travellers set out from Millbrook.

beats.scene: A tall woman with a stick sets the order of march on a road
beats.summary: Isaura takes command and sets the rules of the journey.

beats.scene: A scribe writes by lantern light while a dog sleeps on his boot
beats.summary: At night Pell writes in the Long Memory, and Juniper decides he is a friend.

beats.scene: A long straight road with an old stone milestone at dawn
beats.summary: The party walks the Long Road, and Pell tells how the Beacon Keepers built it.

beats.scene: A farmer sits in the middle of his ripe wheat doing nothing
beats.summary: A farmer has forgotten his harvest, and Corin's gift of bread is left uneaten.

beats.scene: Silent grey-cloaked figures stand in a line on a hill behind the travellers
beats.summary: Juniper growls, and silent grey-cloaked figures, the Hushed, appear on a hill behind the party.

beats.scene: A line of grey figures keeps a steady distance behind four walkers
beats.summary: The Hushed follow all day, never closer and never farther, and Isaura explains who they are.

beats.scene: A warm roadside inn glows with lamplight at dusk
beats.summary: The party reaches the Wheatsheaf inn, where the innkeeper Bess Harker still remembers everything.

beats.scene: Grey figures stand in a silent ring around an inn at night
beats.summary: In the night the Hushed surround the inn, every face turned toward the lantern.

beats.scene: Four travellers escape through a cellar trapdoor into a field of barley
beats.summary: Bess leads the party out through the cellar trapdoor, and they escape into the barley field.

beats.scene: Ancient dark trees close over a narrow path in a deep forest
beats.summary: The Long Road runs into Thornwood, an ancient forest, and narrows to a faint path.

beats.scene: Thorny branches reach across a narrow path and tug at a cloak
beats.summary: Thorns and dead leaves hide the path, and even Isaura admits that they are lost.

beats.scene: Four travellers camp in a dark hollow around a glowing lantern
beats.summary: In the night camp the stars are hidden and the Dawnlight burns lower than before.

beats.scene: A scribe turns the pages of a thick book in a dark forest
beats.summary: Pell recites a forester's map of the wood, but the trees have grown and the paths have shifted.

beats.scene: A lantern's golden flame leans toward a dark gap between old trees
beats.summary: At dawn the Dawnlight's flame leans toward a gap between two oaks.

beats.scene: Four travellers follow a leaning flame through a gap between thorn bushes
beats.summary: The party follows the flame and the thorns draw back, and birds begin to sing.

beats.scene: Rows of straw beehives stand in a sunny forest clearing
beats.summary: The trees open on a sunny clearing full of beehives.

beats.scene: A woman in a straw hat offers honey to four travellers
beats.summary: Marigold Fenn, the beekeeper, gives each of them a spoonful of honey.

beats.scene: A woman in a straw hat speaks beside humming beehives
beats.summary: Marigold tells them that the Grey feeds on forgotten things and hates being remembered.

beats.scene: A beekeeper points along a forest path as bees rise in a golden cloud
beats.summary: Marigold shows the way out of the wood, gives them honeycomb and warns that the Hushed are near.

beats.scene: Grey-cloaked figures close in around four travellers at the edge of a forest
beats.summary: At the forest's edge the Hushed catch up and close a ring around the party.

beats.scene: A scribe holds up a thick book, reading aloud to grey figures
beats.summary: Pell reads out the names of the people of Millbrook from the Long Memory, and the Dawnlight brightens.

beats.scene: A small boy in a grey cloak blinks as his hood slips
beats.summary: At the name of Pip Cobb, one of the Hushed, a small boy, wakes.

beats.scene: A boy cries beside a campfire as a woman wraps a blanket around him
beats.summary: Rook wraps Pip in a blanket by the fire, and he tells them his name.

beats.scene: A boy sits by a fire describing a grey room without corners
beats.summary: Pip describes the Grey as a room with no corners and no door.

beats.scene: Two travellers talk quietly by a dying fire at night
beats.summary: Pell and Isaura decide that a name works best when it comes with a face and a story.

beats.scene: A farmer with a grey mare and a hay cart waves at a roadside
beats.summary: Hob Garrick, a kindly farmer, offers to carry Pip home to Millbrook.

beats.scene: A boy hugs a brown dog goodbye beside a hay cart
beats.summary: Pip says goodbye to Juniper and gives Corin a small blue marble.

beats.scene: Four travellers watch a hay cart roll away down a long road
beats.summary: The party watches the cart go, and Corin wonders how many more are lost.

beats.scene: Four travellers walk toward snowy mountains beneath a pink sunrise
beats.summary: Isaura turns the party toward the Hightarn Pass, one mountain at a time.

beats.scene: Four travellers stand at the foot of a vast snowy mountain
beats.summary: At the foot of the mountains Isaura looks up at Ironcrown and speaks of her husband Tam.

beats.scene: A tall woman hands out ropes, boots and woollen hats
beats.summary: Isaura inspects every pack, hands out boots, hats and rope, and teaches them to walk in snow.

beats.scene: Four travellers and a dog climb a snowy mountain path beneath heavy clouds
beats.summary: The party climbs into the Hightarn Pass as the first snow falls and the path grows steep.

beats.scene: A scribe clings to a rock ledge above a deep drop, eyes shut
beats.summary: Pell, terrified of heights, is walked along a high ledge by Corin.

beats.scene: A woman crosses a narrow ice bridge over a deep crack
beats.summary: Rook crosses a bridge of frozen snow over a crack in the glacier first, and laughs.

beats.scene: A tall woman rubs her knee as snow swirls around her
beats.summary: Isaura's knee hurts again in the cold, and Corin quietly slows the pace.

beats.scene: A blizzard of white snow sweeps across a narrow mountain path
beats.summary: A blizzard strikes, and the party ties itself together with the rope.

beats.scene: Four travellers shelter inside a small stone hut as snow falls
beats.summary: Isaura finds a shepherds' hut, and they shut the door against the storm.

beats.scene: Four travellers sit around a lantern telling stories in a stone hut
beats.summary: To pass the night each tells a story from home: Rook the river, Isaura the mountains, Pell his library, Corin the ferry.

beats.scene: A scribe writes by lantern light as the flame grows taller
beats.summary: Pell sees that the flame grows taller with every story and writes it down.

beats.scene: Four travellers stand in a stone hut doorway before a still white dawn
beats.summary: The storm has gone and the world is white and silent, and Isaura goes out to read the path.

beats.scene: A grey mist creeps over a snowy ridge toward four small figures
beats.summary: At dawn the Grey rolls over the ridge toward the hut, faster than any mist should move.

beats.scene: A tall woman plants a walking stick in snow and spreads her arms
beats.summary: Isaura steps between the mist and the others and tells them to hold the light high.

beats.scene: A grey mist wraps around a tall woman standing in the snow
beats.summary: The Grey passes over Isaura, and the Dawnlight flares a moment too late.

beats.scene: A gruff old woman stares blankly while her friends watch, dismayed
beats.summary: Isaura has forgotten her name, her mountains and her friends, and asks who they are.

beats.scene: Corin ties a rope gently around a confused old woman on a snowy track
beats.summary: Isaura wanders off down the path, and Corin gently ties a rope around her waist.

beats.scene: Two travellers help an old woman up a steep snowy slope
beats.summary: Rook and Corin half carry Isaura up the slope toward the top of the pass.

beats.scene: A scribe frantically turns the pages of a thick book in snow
beats.summary: Pell hunts through the Long Memory for any help, filled with shame.

beats.scene: A scribe reads aloud from an old page by lantern light
beats.summary: Pell finds an old Keeper's note: a name spoken by someone who loves the person may bring them back.

beats.scene: Three travellers sit around a small fire in a shallow cave
beats.summary: The party shelters in a cave beneath the summit and promises not to leave without Isaura.

beats.scene: Three travellers sit by a cave fire watching a gruff old woman
beats.summary: Rook says that if a name can bring Isaura back, they must give her every memory they have of her.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf speaks gently to a puzzled old woman
beats.summary: Rook says Isaura's full name and title, but Isaura only nods politely.

beats.scene: A boy tells an old woman a story she once told
beats.summary: Corin retells the story Isaura told in the hut, about finding a lost child on Ironcrown with Tam.

beats.scene: A scribe recites a story word for word beside a cave fire
beats.summary: Pell recites the story exactly as Isaura told it, and the Dawnlight burns higher.

beats.scene: An old woman strokes a brown dog resting its chin on her knee
beats.summary: Juniper lays her chin on Isaura's knee, and Isaura murmurs the name Bramble.

beats.scene: A boy points from a cave mouth to a great peak in the sunrise
beats.summary: Corin shows Isaura Ironcrown in the sunrise and says she has walked every path on it.

beats.scene: An old woman weeps in a cave mouth, looking at a great peak
beats.summary: Isaura whispers the mountain's name and then Tam's, and weeps.

beats.scene: An old woman laughs and hugs three travellers in a cave
beats.summary: Isaura's memory returns: she declares her name and complains about her knee.

beats.scene: An old woman speaks seriously beside a small fire
beats.summary: Isaura says the Grey was like a cold, empty room, and that she heard someone weeping far away.

beats.scene: Four travellers descend a rocky hillside above a vast shining white plain
beats.summary: The party leaves the cave and descends, and the Salt Flats appear below like a mirror.

beats.scene: A tall woman leads three travellers down a stony mountain path
beats.summary: Isaura leads the descent with long strides and lectures them about the plain below.

beats.scene: Posts of white salt mark a path across a shining white plain
beats.summary: The Salt Road begins, marked by white posts across a plain as bright as a mirror.

beats.scene: Four travellers walk across a glaring white plain with scarves over their faces
beats.summary: They cross the glare all day, and Isaura repeats her one rule: follow the posts.

beats.scene: Four travellers sleep beside a salt rock under a sky of stars
beats.summary: At night they camp beside a block of rock salt under a sky full of stars.

beats.scene: A boy walks alone across a moonlit white plain carrying a lantern
beats.summary: In the night Corin rises in his sleep and walks away from the camp, with Juniper following.

beats.scene: A boy sees his mother waving in a doorway of a shimmering cottage
beats.summary: Ahead, Saltreach shimmers on the plain, and his mother waves from the cottage door.

beats.scene: A boy slows down on white ground, his lantern heavy in his arms
beats.summary: A soft voice tells him to rest, and the lantern grows heavy.

beats.scene: A dog tugs a boy's sleeve while a lantern flares
beats.summary: Juniper bites his sleeve, and the Dawnlight flares, breaking the voice.

beats.scene: A shimmering village dissolves into white salt and grey mist
beats.summary: The vision melts away, and Corin is alone and far from the road.

beats.scene: Three travellers sit together on a white plain at night
beats.summary: The others find him, and Rook says that the Grey does not lie but offers what you most want.

beats.scene: Four travellers crest a sandy dune above a wide grey sea
beats.summary: At the far edge of the plain, the travellers smell the sea, and Corin sees it for the first time.

beats.scene: A grey harbour town with a dark lighthouse stands above crowded boats
beats.summary: They reach Port Larrow, a harbour town with a dark lighthouse and no lights in its streets.

beats.scene: Fishing boats lie tied up and sailors wander slowly along a stone quay
beats.summary: Boats lie idle and nets rot, and sailors wander the quay with nowhere to go.

beats.scene: A tall woman points a stick at a dark lighthouse on a black hill
beats.summary: Isaura tells how the lighthouse once guided ships along the coast, on the hill of the Larrowhead Beacon.

beats.scene: A young woman with a sailmaker's needle runs down a cobbled street
beats.summary: Tilda Vane, a sailmaker, begs them to help her light the lighthouse again.

beats.scene: Four travellers climb a spiral stone stair past a silent seated man
beats.summary: Tilda leads them up the tower, past her father Osric, who has been taken by the Grey.

beats.scene: A golden lantern lights the lamp room of a great lighthouse
beats.summary: Corin lights the lighthouse lamp from the Dawnlight.

beats.scene: A beam of golden light sweeps across a dark harbour and sea
beats.summary: The beam sweeps over the harbour, and the Grey draws back from the town.

beats.scene: Townspeople cheer on a harbour quay beneath a lighthouse beam
beats.summary: The people cheer, and the sailors begin to call out the names of their boats.

beats.scene: Four travellers eat fish stew in a warm harbour inn at night
beats.summary: At the Fisher's Rest Corin cannot sleep, knowing that one lamp can hold the fog back only for a night.

beats.scene: Grey mist creeps between the last houses of a harbour town at dawn
beats.summary: In the morning the Grey is back at the town's edges, and Tilda says her lamp oil is nearly gone.

beats.scene: A silent sailor on a quay speaks in a strange, deep voice
beats.summary: A silent sailor speaks in a voice that is not his own, and the whole quay listens.

beats.scene: A grey-cloaked sailor speaks courteously to a boy holding a lantern
beats.summary: The voice greets Corin by name and offers him rest if he gives up the Dawnlight.

beats.scene: A boy answers a hollow-eyed sailor firmly as friends stand behind him
beats.summary: Corin refuses without anger, and says that he is listening.

beats.scene: A sailor kneels on wet stones as grey mist drains from the quay
beats.summary: The voice says Corin may come to Cairnhead if he dares, and the sailor falls to his knees.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf studies boats along a crowded quay
beats.summary: The coast roads are thick with Grey, so Rook looks for a boat, though she fears the sea.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat with a patched grey sail rocks beside a quay
beats.summary: Tilda gives them her grandfather's boat, the Heron.

beats.scene: A boy sews a torn grey sail with a bone needle on a quay
beats.summary: Corin mends the torn sail with his mother's needle and cord.

beats.scene: Townspeople load sacks of bread and barrels onto a small boat
beats.summary: The people of Port Larrow bring bread, water, rope and a brass compass for the voyage.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat leaves harbour at dusk beneath a sweeping lighthouse beam
beats.summary: At dusk the Heron sails out, with Rook at the tiller and Tilda waving.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat with a grey sail glides across a clear moonlit sea
beats.summary: On the first night the Heron sails smoothly, and Isaura is seasick.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf steers a boat as porpoises leap beside it
beats.summary: The next day is bright, porpoises leap beside the boat, and Rook admits she has missed the sea.

beats.scene: Two young people sit at a boat's bow under a starry sky
beats.summary: At night Pell names the stars for Corin, and Corin says he would be lost without him.

beats.scene: A low grey fog bank stands like a wall across a dark sea
beats.summary: On the third morning a fog bank stands ahead that does not move with the wind.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat rocks in a storm under thick grey fog at sea
beats.summary: The Heron sails into the fog, and a storm breaks over the boat.

beats.scene: A brass compass needle spins wildly in a boy's cold hand
beats.summary: The compass needle spins, because the Grey has confused it.

beats.scene: A boy steers a small boat by the leaning flame of a lantern
beats.summary: Corin sees the Dawnlight lean in his hand and steers the boat by it.

beats.scene: Waves wash across a small boat's deck as a dog braces under a seat
beats.summary: Great waves wash over the deck, and Isaura ties everyone to the mast.

beats.scene: A boy and a woman hold a tiller together in heavy rain
beats.summary: Rook takes the helm beside Corin and laughs, no longer afraid of the sea.

beats.scene: A small boat glides toward a tall cliff crowned by a ruined tower
beats.summary: At dawn the storm ends, and a cliff with a ruined tower appears: Cairnhead.

beats.scene: A small sailing boat lands in a rocky cove beneath a tall cliff
beats.summary: The Heron lands in a cove at the foot of Cairnhead, and Rook laughs with relief.

beats.scene: Four travellers rest on a pebble beach and look up at a ruined tower
beats.summary: They rest on the pebbles and look up at the ruined tower at the top of the cliff.

beats.scene: A narrow stair cut into a cliff face with small stone lamp niches
beats.summary: Isaura finds the old stair cut into the cliff, with empty lamp niches at every turn.

beats.scene: Four climbers and a dog climb a narrow stone stair cut into a cliff
beats.summary: They begin the climb with the sea booming below them.

beats.scene: A scribe counts steps aloud on a narrow cliff stair
beats.summary: Pell counts the steps to keep his mind off the drop, and loses count.

beats.scene: A grey mist creeps up a cliff stair behind four climbers
beats.summary: The Grey creeps up the stair behind them, step by step.

beats.scene: A woman ties a rope around herself and a limping old woman
beats.summary: Isaura's knee fails her, and Rook ties a rope around them both to help her.

beats.scene: Four travellers rest in a ruined stone watch-house with carved words on its wall
beats.summary: Halfway up they rest in a ruined watch-house, where carved words read: Keep the light, keep the name.

beats.scene: Grey-cloaked figures climb a cliff stair in a long line far below
beats.summary: Looking down, they see dozens of the Hushed climbing the stair below them.

beats.scene: Four travellers stand before a broken stone gate at the top of a cliff
beats.summary: The Dawnlight burns brighter, and the stair ends at a broken gate at the summit.

beats.scene: A ruined tower and a dark stone Beacon bowl on a windswept cliff top
beats.summary: At the summit of Cairnhead the travellers find the broken tower and the cold stone bowl of the first Beacon.

beats.scene: A tall figure of drifting fog stands before a dark stone Beacon
beats.summary: Beside the Beacon stands the Pale Regent, a tall figure of fog who wears a Keeper's chain.

beats.scene: Grey-cloaked figures gather at the edge of a windswept cliff top
beats.summary: The Hushed come up the stair and gather silently at the edge of the cliff, keeping their distance.

beats.scene: A misty figure speaks softly to a boy holding a lantern
beats.summary: The Regent says that long ago he was Ansel Dray, Keeper of this very Beacon.

beats.scene: A misty figure gazes at an empty stone bowl as the wind drops
beats.summary: Ansel tells how his wife Lena and his daughter Wren died in a winter sickness, and the Beacon could not save them.

beats.scene: A tall figure of fog touches a silver chain at his neck
beats.summary: Ansel stopped lighting the fire, and when the pain stayed, he asked the Grey to take it away.

beats.scene: A misty figure opens his hands as pale mist rises from them
beats.summary: He believes the Grey is a mercy, a place where nobody weeps.

beats.scene: A tall woman stares at a misty figure with recognition
beats.summary: Isaura says that she heard someone weeping inside the Grey, and that it was he.

beats.scene: A misty figure holds out a pale hand toward a boy holding a lantern
beats.summary: The Regent asks Corin kindly for the Dawnlight, and promises to keep it safe.

beats.scene: A boy shakes his head, holding a lantern against his chest
beats.summary: Corin refuses without anger, because he promised an old man under a willow.

beats.scene: Four friends and a dog stand in a circle around a lantern
beats.summary: Corin sets the Dawnlight on the stones, and the friends form a circle around it.

beats.scene: A woman in a red scarf speaks softly beside a glowing lantern
beats.summary: Rook tells of her mother singing to her on the river, and the flame brightens.

beats.scene: A tall old woman tells a story beside a lantern, shadows drawing in
beats.summary: Isaura tells of Tam and the lamp they lit every night in their hut window.

beats.scene: A thin young scribe speaks beside a lantern with his book closed
beats.summary: Pell tells of the library and his teacher Orla Finch, and names every reader he knew.

beats.scene: A boy and a dog speak and bark beside a blazing lantern
beats.summary: Corin tells of Aldous, his mother, his father and the ferry, and Juniper barks.

beats.scene: A misty figure flinches as threads of fog drift from his feet
beats.summary: The Regent flinches, his fog thins, and the Hushed stir at the cliff edge.

beats.scene: A boy speaks gently to a tall figure of thinning mist
beats.summary: Corin tells the Regent that remembering a sorrow is not the same as being broken by it.

beats.scene: A boy holds out a bright lantern in both hands to a misty figure
beats.summary: Corin offers the Dawnlight to the Regent, not to be taken but to be shared.

beats.scene: A misty figure's eyes fill with tears in lantern light
beats.summary: Ansel remembers his name and the names of Lena and Wren, and the sound of Lena's laugh.

beats.scene: A misty figure kneels and lays a silver chain at a boy's feet
beats.summary: The Regent kneels, weeps, and lays his Keeper's chain at Corin's feet.

beats.scene: A boy lifts a glowing lantern to an old stone Beacon at sunrise
beats.summary: At sunrise Corin lifts the Dawnlight to the great stone bowl of the Beacon.

beats.scene: A great golden fire roars up from a stone Beacon on a cliff
beats.summary: The Beacon catches with a roar of golden fire.

beats.scene: A chain of golden fires lights up across dark hills
beats.summary: Far away on the Hightarn a fire answers, and then others leap up across the land.

beats.scene: Seven golden fires burn across a whole country from sea to mountains
beats.summary: Pell names the seven Beacons as they light, and Aldermoor is joined again by fire.

beats.scene: Sunrise over a blue sea as the last grey fog melts away
beats.summary: As the sun climbs, the Grey melts from the sea and the sky.

beats.scene: People in grey cloaks lift their faces to the sunrise on a clifftop
beats.summary: The Hushed wake, speak their names and remember the people they love.

beats.scene: A Keeper in a silver chain tends a roaring fire beside a stone bowl
beats.summary: Ansel decides to stay as Keeper of Cairnhead and promises to tell the true story of the Grey.

beats.scene: A father and daughter embrace on a harbour quay beneath a lighthouse
beats.summary: The friends sail home to Port Larrow, where Osric Vane wakes and Tilda runs to him.

beats.scene: A woman runs down a lane toward a boy and a dog
beats.summary: After partings at Millbrook, Corin reaches Saltreach and his mother runs down the lane to meet him.

beats.scene: A boy hangs a glowing lantern in the high window of a stone tower
beats.summary: Corin hangs the Dawnlight in the Tower of Aldermoor, no longer the last lantern but the first of many.

A1A2: At dawn, Corin Thatch pushed the flat ferry across the river at Saltreach.
His brown dog Juniper sat at the front and watched every passenger.
At home, his mother Mara sat by the window and fixed fishing nets.
Each morning, old Tobias the fisherman crossed the river and talked with Corin.
On market day, some traders said a grey fog had swallowed a town.
That night, old Wenna told the children a story about seven great fires.
One evening, the birds stopped singing, and a grey cloud lay on the horizon.
The whole village stood on the landing and watched the grey cloud come closer.
That night, the fog moved through the village like slow, cold smoke.
In the morning, Tobias stood outside his house and could not remember his name.
The healer Nan Pruitt came, but Tobias had no fever and no pain.
Corin said his name again and again, but Tobias only smiled.
At the village meeting, Mara said, “Keep a lamp in every window.”
Late that night, Corin and Juniper went to check the ferry ropes.
Suddenly an old man in a torn cloak stepped out of the fog.
The old man was Brother Aldous, and the golden glow pushed the fog away.
In the middle of the river, Aldous opened his cloak and showed a lantern.
He said the seven great fires had gone out, one after another.
Aldous warned that the Grey wanted the light and would never stop looking.
Aldous showed Corin a map and pointed to a cliff called Cairnhead.
On the far bank, Aldous sat down under a tall willow tree.
For forty years, he had kept the lantern safe in the Tower of Aldermoor.
The flame bent toward Corin's hand like a flower toward the sun.
Corin shook his head and said, “I am only a boy with a ferry.”
Aldous smiled and said that a river is crossed one push at a time.
Aldous gave Corin the lantern and said, “Never leave it alone in the dark.”
Then the old man closed his eyes and fell into a deep sleep.
At dawn, Corin and the villagers buried Aldous under the willow tree.
At home, Corin showed his mother the lantern and told her everything.
Mara was quiet for a long time, and then she said, “Go.”
Mara packed bread, cheese and warm socks into an old leather bag.
She also gave him her net needle and a coil of strong cord.
Many villagers came to the lane with lamps to say goodbye.
Mara kissed Corin goodbye at the door, and the fog gathered behind them.
Corin and Juniper left Saltreach and walked along the river path.
Corin looked back once, and the village was almost lost in the fog.
That night, he slept under a tree with the lantern close beside him.
The next morning, a woman in a red scarf waved at him from a barge.
Her name was Rook, and she said river people always help each other.
Rook agreed to carry Corin down the river to the town of Millbrook.
The Grey followed them along the bank, but the light pushed it back.
Rook showed Corin how to steer the big barge down the river.
That night, Rook told Corin how the seven fires were first lit.
Each fire had its own name, and each one watched over a valley.
Rook said she once sailed on the sea, but now she loved the river.
They passed a village where silent people stood on the bank and watched.
Rook stopped the barge in the middle of the river for the night.
Corin dreamed of Aldous, and the lantern flame shook in the dark.
In the morning, smoke from many mills rose above a town ahead.
The Kestrel reached Millbrook, a busy town with a big stone dock.
The market in Millbrook was full of people, noise and good smells.
One baker could not remember the price of her own bread.
Rook said, “I know rivers, but I do not know mountains.”
At a stall, a tall woman with a stick was reading a map.
She was Isaura Brack, and she said she was too old to guide anyone.
Suddenly, a thief in a dark cloak grabbed at the lantern.
A young man with a big book hit the thief, and he fell down.
The thief jumped up and ran away between the stalls.
The young man was Pell, and he never forgot anything he read.
Pell asked to come, and Isaura said yes, because her sore knee felt better.
Rook gave her barge to her cousin, and the friends began to walk.
Isaura made a rule: walk slowly, rest often, and never leave the road.
At night, Pell wrote in his book while Juniper slept beside him.
The Long Road was old and straight, with a stone every mile.
In a field, a farmer sat in his wheat and forgot to cut it.
On a hill behind them, grey figures stood silent and still.
The grey figures followed them all day, never closer and never farther.
That evening, they found a warm inn, and the owner gave them soup.
In the night, grey figures stood in a circle around the inn.
The friends escaped through a small door under the floor and ran away.
The Long Road led them into Thornwood, an old and very dark forest.
Thorns pulled at their coats, and soon the path was gone.
That night, no stars shone, and strange sounds came from the trees.
Pell read from a book about the forest, but the paths had changed.
Then the flame of the lantern leaned toward a gap between the trees.
They followed the flame, and the thorns slowly moved out of the way.
Suddenly they walked into a sunny clearing full of busy bees.
A woman in a straw hat gave them honey and a smile.
Marigold said the Grey eats forgotten things and hates being remembered.
Marigold showed them the way out of the forest and gave them a sweet gift.
At the edge of the forest, the grey figures caught up with them.
Pell stood up and read the names of people from Millbrook.
Then one grey figure, a small boy, blinked and looked around.
The boy was named Pip, and he cried beside the warm fire.
He said the Grey was like a room with no corners.
Pell said that a name works best when you know the person.
A kind farmer named Hob came by with a cart and a horse.
Pip said goodbye to Juniper and gave Corin a small blue marble.
They watched the cart roll away, and Corin felt both happy and sad.
Then they turned toward the mountains, where snow shone in the morning light.
They reached the foot of the mountains, where the air was cold and clean.
Isaura gave everyone strong boots, warm hats and a long rope.
Slowly, the party climbed the steep path, and soft snow began to fall.
Pell was afraid of high places, so Corin held his hand.
Rook went first across a narrow bridge of ice over a deep crack.
Isaura's knee hurt, but she said nothing, and Corin walked more slowly.
Then a great storm came, and the wind and snow were wild.
They found a small stone hut and ran inside just in time.
To pass the night, each friend told a story from home.
With every story, the flame of the lantern grew a little taller.
In the morning, the storm was gone, and the world was white and quiet.
Suddenly, a grey mist came over the mountain ridge toward them.
Isaura stepped in front of the others and held up her stick.
The Grey touched her, and she stood very still in the snow.
Then Isaura smiled at them and said, “Who are you all?”
She tried to walk away alone, so they gently tied her to the rope.
Rook and Corin held her arms and helped her climb over the pass.
Pell turned the pages of his book again and again, but found nothing.
Pell found an old note: the voice of a friend can call someone back.
They found a cave, lit a fire, and sat close beside Isaura.
Rook said, “We must help her remember who she is.”
Rook said her name gently, but Isaura only smiled politely.
Corin told her the story she had told them in the hut.
Pell said the story again, word for word, just as she told it.
Juniper put her head on Isaura's knee, and Isaura stroked her ears.
Corin pointed to the great white peak outside and said its name.
“Ironcrown,” whispered Isaura, and her eyes slowly became bright again.
Then she laughed and said, “I am Isaura Brack, and my knee hurts!”
She told them the Grey was like a cold, empty room.
Together, they walked down the mountain toward a huge white plain.
Isaura led the way down the stony path, strong and happy.
White posts of salt showed the way across the great white plain.
They walked all day, and the white ground shone like a mirror.
At night, they slept beside a big rock under a sky of stars.
Corin woke up and walked alone across the white ground.
He saw Saltreach ahead, and his mother waved from the door.
He felt very tired, and the lantern felt heavy in his arms.
Juniper bit his sleeve, and the lantern flared with bright light.
The village turned into white salt and grey mist, and he saw the trick.
The others found him, and Rook said, “The Grey offers what you want.”
At the end of the plain, they smelled the salty sea.
They came to Port Larrow, a grey harbour town with a dark lighthouse.
The sailors walked slowly on the dock with nowhere to go.
The big lighthouse stood dark, and no light shone for the boats.
A young woman named Tilda came and asked them to light the lighthouse.
They climbed the long stone stairs inside the tall lighthouse.
At the top, Corin lit the big lamp with the Dawnlight.
A golden beam swept across the harbour and the dark sea.
All the people in the town came out and cheered.
That night, they slept at an inn, but Corin could not sleep.
In the morning, the grey mist came back to the edge of the town.
A silent sailor on the dock suddenly spoke in a strange, deep voice.
The voice said, “Give me the light, and you can rest.”
Corin said, “No,” and his friends stood close behind him.
The voice sounded sad, and then the sailor fell to his knees.
The only way to Cairnhead was by sea, so Rook looked for a boat.
She found a small boat called the Heron, and Tilda gave it to them.
Corin used his mother's needle to mend the torn grey sail.
The people of the town brought bread, water and rope for the trip.
At dusk, the little boat sailed out, and the lighthouse beam shone behind it.
That night, Isaura felt sick from the waves, and she held the rail.
The next day was bright, and happy dolphins jumped beside the boat.
At night, Pell and Corin watched the stars and talked quietly.
Ahead of them, a thick grey fog lay on the sea.
Soon, a big storm hit the Heron, and the wind was very strong.
The compass needle went round and round and showed no direction.
Corin watched the lantern flame, which leaned toward the right way.
Big waves washed over the deck, and Juniper held on tightly.
Rook helped Corin hold the boat steady, and she was not afraid.
At dawn, the storm ended, and they saw a tall cliff with a tower.
The Heron landed on a small beach under the tall cliff.
They rested on the beach and looked up at the old tower.
Isaura found a stone stair cut into the side of the cliff.
They climbed the narrow stair, and the wind blew hard.
Pell counted the steps aloud, and soon he lost count.
Behind them, the grey fog began to climb the stairs.
Isaura's knee hurt, so Rook held her arm and helped her up.
On a wall, someone had carved: “Keep the light, keep the name.”
Far below, many grey figures began to climb the stairs.
Near the top, the lantern shone brighter, and they reached the old gate.
At the top, they found an old tower and a great stone bowl.
A tall figure made of fog stood before the dark Beacon.
The grey figures from the stairs came up and stood at the edge.
The figure said that long ago, he was a Keeper named Ansel Dray.
Ansel's wife and daughter died in a cold winter, and he was very sad.
He lit the Beacon every night, but it could not save them.
He wanted the whole world to forget its pain, so he joined the Grey.
Isaura said that she had heard him crying when the Grey took her.
Ansel held out his pale hand and asked Corin for the lantern.
Corin said no, but he was not angry, and he did not move.
Corin set the lantern on the stones, and his friends stood in a circle.
Rook told about her mother, who sang to her on the river.
Isaura told about Tam, and the lamp in the window of their hut.
Pell told about the library, and the smell of old books.
Corin told about Aldous, his mother, and the ferry at dawn.
The more they told, the brighter the flame grew, and the fog shook.
Corin told the Regent that remembering sadness is not the same as being broken.
Then Corin held out the lantern to the Regent with both hands.
Slowly, the Regent remembered his name, and Lena's laugh, and Wren's songs.
He cried, and he laid his silver chain at Corin's feet.
At sunrise, Corin lifted the Dawnlight to the great stone bowl of the Beacon.
The Beacon caught fire with a roar and shone like gold.
Far away, the other six Beacons lit, one after another.
Soon the whole country was shining with golden light.
At dawn, the Grey melted away from the land and the sea.
The Hushed woke up and remembered their names and the people they loved.
Ansel decided to stay and keep the Beacon, and he thanked Corin.
They sailed home, and in Port Larrow, Tilda hugged her father again.
At last, Corin came home to Saltreach, and his mother ran to meet him.
Corin hung the lantern in the Tower, the first of many lights.
B1B2: Corin Thatch is fifteen years old, and every morning at dawn he poles the flat ferry across the slow river at Saltreach. The marsh is quiet then, with mist on the water and only the cry of the herons.
Juniper, his brown dog, rides at the front of the ferry and knows every passenger by their smell. She wags her tail for the people she likes, and she growls softly at anyone she does not trust.
In the evening Corin goes home to the small cottage where his mother Mara mends the village's fishing nets. His father, Davin, ran the ferry once, but he died of a winter fever when Corin was seven.
Every day the same people wait on the wooden landing with their baskets, and old Tobias the fisherman is always the first. Corin is a quiet boy, but he always has a kind word for them.
On market day, a group of traders arrive in Saltreach with strange news from the east. They say that a grey fog has been rolling across the land, and that whole towns have vanished inside it.

That evening, Granny Wenna, the oldest woman in the village, tells the children the story of the seven Beacons. The children laugh and say it is only a tale, but Corin notices that she does not smile.
At sunset, the marsh birds suddenly rise into the sky and then fall silent, one flock after another. Far away, along the edge of the horizon, lies a long grey bank that was not there the day before.
The whole village gathers on the landing to watch the grey wall slowly move closer across the marsh. Someone rings the old bell, but nobody knows what to do, and Corin holds Juniper close.

That night, Corin cannot sleep, and he sits by the window with his dog while the fog creeps into the village. It slides along the lane without a sound, and it is colder than any mist he has ever known.
In the morning, the fog is thinner, but old Tobias stands in front of his own front door and does not go in. He looks at the house as if he has never seen it, and he cannot remember his own name.
All morning the villagers crowd around Tobias, and Nan Pruitt, the healer, examines him carefully. She finds no fever and no wound, and his grandchildren cry because he does not know their names.
Corin kneels in front of the old man and tells him his own name, over and over again. Tobias only smiles politely, and by noon, three more people in the same lane have forgotten who they are.

That evening the villagers meet in the old hall, and they argue about whether to flee the marsh or stay. Mara stands up and says that a lamp must burn in every window, but in the thick fog every flame burns low and weak.

Late that night Corin cannot bear the silence, so he takes Juniper down to the landing to check the ferry's ropes. The dog stops at the water's edge, whining, and stares into the darkness as if she hears something.
Out of the fog an old man in a torn grey cloak staggers onto the landing, leaning heavily on a stick. He begs Corin to take him across the river, and a warm golden light glows faintly under his coat.
Corin helps him onto the ferry and pushes off into the dark, and the fog draws back from the little boat. The old man says his name is Brother Aldous Wick, and that he has come a very long way.

Halfway across the river, Aldous opens his cloak and shows a small lantern with a flame as bright as a morning star. “This is the Dawnlight,” he says quietly, “and it is the last lantern in all of Aldermoor.”

Aldous explains that there were once seven Beacons, great fires that burned on hills and cliffs across the land. One by one, they went dark, and since then the Grey has crept further into Aldermoor every year.

The old man glances nervously at the river bank, where grey shapes stand silent in the mist. He warns Corin that the Grey hunts the light, because the Dawnlight is the one flame that will never go out by itself.

Aldous unrolls a worn map and points to a tall cliff on the coast called Cairnhead. If the Dawnlight is carried there, he says, it can light the first and greatest Beacon again, and the others will follow.

They reach the far bank, and Aldous sinks down against the trunk of an old willow, breathing hard. Corin spreads his own coat over the old man's knees, and Juniper lies down beside him to keep him warm.
Aldous tells Corin about the Tower of Aldermoor, an old stone tower in the hills upriver. He kept the Dawnlight there for forty years, until the Grey came close enough to reach the tower's door.

The old man holds out the lantern, and the flame leans gently toward Corin's hand, like a flower turning toward the sun. Juniper wags her tail, because she knows that something important is happening.
Corin steps back and shakes his head, because he cannot believe that the lantern has chosen him. He says that he is only a ferryman's son, and that someone braver and cleverer should carry it.
Aldous smiles and tells him that a ferryman knows something that heroes often forget. A river is crossed one push of the pole at a time, he says, and the light needs a friend, not a hero.
At last Corin takes the lantern, and it feels warm and light in his hands, like a living thing. “Never leave it alone in the dark,” says Aldous, “and never give it to anyone who only asks sweetly.”

Aldous leans his head against the willow and closes his eyes, and a peaceful smile spreads across his face. Corin waits beside him all night with Juniper, but the old man falls into a deep sleep and does not wake.

At dawn, Corin crosses the river and brings the carpenter Wilf Gorse and some of the villagers who still remember him. Together they bury Brother Aldous beneath the willow, and Corin places a flat grey stone over the grave.
At home, Corin puts the Dawnlight on the kitchen table and tells his mother everything that happened. Mara listens without a word, and the golden light moves softly across her tired face.
For a long time Mara says nothing, and she looks at the lantern and then at her son. Then she says quietly that the fog will reach their door too, and that somebody must go.
Mara works all night, packing a leather bag with bread, cheese, dried apples and thick woollen socks. Corin watches her fold each thing carefully, as if she could fold her worry into the bag as well.
Before dawn, she presses her own net-mending needle and a coil of strong cord into his hand. It is the most useful thing she owns, she says, and she wants it to travel with him.

News spreads quickly, and by sunrise the villagers who still remember their names have gathered in the lane with lamps. Wilf Gorse shakes Corin's hand, Nan Pruitt gives him a small pot of healing salve, and the old bell rings once.
At the cottage door, Mara holds her son tightly and kisses his forehead, and she does not cry until he turns away. Behind them, the pale fog gathers at the end of the lane, waiting.
Corin walks out of Saltreach with Juniper at his heels and the lantern swinging gently from his hand. The path follows the river, and soon the roofs of the village are small behind him.
Once he looks back, and he sees the village fading into the fog like a picture left out in the rain. Then he lifts the lantern higher, and the grey mist on the path draws back from its light.
That night Corin makes camp under a hawthorn tree, and he lies awake for a long time. The lantern burns steadily beside him, and Juniper rests her chin on his arm, which makes him feel less alone.

In the morning the path comes down to the river again, where a barge with a patched red sail is drifting slowly with the current. A woman in a red scarf stands at the tiller, and she waves cheerfully at the boy and his dog.

She introduces herself as Rook Tarn, and she asks what a boy and a dog are doing alone on the Wendle path. When Corin says he has no money, she laughs and says that river people never charge each other for a ride.

Rook listens to his story, and she looks at the lantern for a long time before she makes up her mind. She agrees to carry him down to Millbrook, and soon the Kestrel casts off and slips into the current.
All that day the Grey follows the barge along the river bank, like a patient animal. Each time it comes close, the Dawnlight shines more brightly and pushes it back like a wall.
Rook is a good teacher, and she lets Corin take the tiller on the long, straight stretches of the river. He learns quickly, because a ferryman already understands currents and sandbars.

After dark, with the lantern standing between them on the deck, Rook tells Corin how the Beacons were first lit. Long ago, she says, the people of Aldermoor were tired of losing their travellers to the dark.

She counts the seven Beacons on her fingers: Cairnhead, Hightarn, Longmere, Thornhill, Millhill, Larrowhead and Marshend. Each one stood in its own valley, and a Keeper lit it every evening at sunset.
Rook admits that she once worked on a seagoing ship, and that she left the sea after a terrible storm. Now she says the river is gentler, because she can always see the bank.
On the second afternoon they pass a small village where dozens of people stand along the bank. None of them speaks or waves, and they all turn their faces slowly to follow the barge.
That night Rook anchors the Kestrel in the middle of the river, far from either bank. She takes the first watch herself, and she does not look at all sleepy.
In the night Corin dreams that Aldous is sitting under the willow tree, saying something he cannot hear. He wakes with a start to find the lantern flickering, and Juniper pressing close against him.
At sunrise, the grey light shows a river bend ahead, and smoke is rising from tall chimneys. Rook points and says that this is Millbrook, the biggest town on the Wendle.
By midmorning the Kestrel glides under a stone bridge and ties up at a busy quay. Corin has never seen so many people in one place, and many of them seem tired and strangely forgetful.

Corin follows Rook through the market, where stalls overflow with wool, apples and coils of rope. The noise is dizzying for a boy from a quiet marsh village, and he holds the lantern close under his coat.

At a bakery stall, the baker stares at her own loaves and cannot remember what they cost. Farther on, the town crier reads the same notice three times, as if he has forgotten that he has just read it.
Rook points to a line of white mountains in the far distance and says that they need a guide. She knows rivers and harbours, she admits, but she knows nothing about snow.

In a corner of the market, a tall weathered woman with a walking stick is studying a map pinned to a stall. Rook whispers that this is Dame Isaura Brack, who guided travellers over the mountains for thirty years.
Corin explains where he needs to go, but Isaura folds her arms and shakes her head. She says that she is retired, that her knee is bad, and that she has no wish to freeze on a mountain.
Suddenly a thief in a dark cloak darts out of the crowd and grabs at the lantern. Corin holds on with both hands, and the people nearby scatter in alarm.
A young man with ink on his fingers swings a thick leather book and knocks the thief to the ground. The thief lets go of the lantern, and the book makes a sound like a slamming door.
The thief scrambles to his feet and runs off between the stalls, and Isaura's stick trips him twice on the way. As he goes, he shouts that a grey voice promised him bread if he brought the light.

The young man is Pell Ainsley, a scribe from the Millbrook library, and the book in his hands is called the Long Memory. He tells them that he forgets nothing he has ever read, and that today this feels more like a burden than a gift.
Pell asks to join them, because the Grey has already taken his teacher and half of the library. Isaura sighs and agrees, and she notices, without saying a word, that her knee has stopped hurting.
Rook leaves the Kestrel in the care of her cousin Dunstan, who works at the Millbrook dock. She pats the rail one last time, and then the four travellers and the dog set out along the road.
Isaura takes command at once, and she announces her rules for the journey. They will walk slowly, rest often, and no one is allowed to complain about blisters before the third day.
At night around the fire, Pell writes in the Long Memory by the light of the Dawnlight. Juniper has decided that he is a friend, and she falls asleep with her head on his boot.
The Long Road is old and perfectly straight, and a grey stone marks every mile. Pell tells them that the Beacon Keepers built it, so that travellers could always find their way between the fires.
They pass a farm where a farmer sits in the middle of his ripe wheat, doing nothing at all. Corin gives him some bread, but the man only thanks him politely and forgets to eat it.
On the third afternoon, Juniper stops and growls, and Corin turns to look back along the road. On a low hill far behind them stand a dozen silent figures in grey cloaks.

The grey figures follow them all day, and they never come closer and never fall farther behind. Isaura says they are the Hushed, people taken by the Grey, who now follow the light like moths following a candle.

At dusk they reach an inn called the Wheatsheaf, and the innkeeper, Bess Harker, still remembers everything. She feeds them hot soup and warm bread, and she tells them that half of her neighbours have forgotten how to speak.

Late that night, Juniper wakes Corin with a low growl, and he looks out of the window. Dozens of grey figures stand in a perfect circle around the inn, without a sound, and every face is turned toward the lantern.

Bess leads them down to the cellar and opens a trapdoor that leads out into the barley field. They crawl out one by one into the darkness, and they run until the inn is only a faint light behind them.
The Long Road runs straight into Thornwood, an ancient forest where the trees grow so thick that the daylight turns green. Soon the road becomes a narrow path, and the path becomes a rumour.
Thorny branches reach across the way and tug at their coats, and the path disappears under a carpet of dead leaves. After an hour, even Isaura has to admit that they are lost.
That night they make camp in a hollow, but no stars shine through the roof of branches. Strange creaks and whispers come from the trees, and Corin notices that the Dawnlight burns lower than before.

Pell opens the Long Memory and recites a forester's map of the wood, with every turn and every stream. Unfortunately, the trees have grown and the paths have shifted, and nothing he remembers matches what they see.

At dawn Corin lifts the lantern, and the golden flame leans gently toward a dark gap between two old oaks. Isaura raises an eyebrow, but she says that a lost traveller should follow any sign she is given.
They follow the leaning flame through the gap, and the thorns seem to draw back on either side. Birds begin to sing somewhere above them, and the air smells of flowers instead of damp earth.
After an hour the trees open suddenly, and they step into a sunny clearing full of straw beehives. Thousands of bees drift lazily through the warm air, humming a low and peaceful tune.
A woman in a straw hat comes out of a small cottage, wiping her hands on her apron. She introduces herself as Marigold Fenn, and she gives each of them a spoonful of golden honey.

While they eat, Marigold tells them that the Grey feeds on forgotten things, and that it hates being remembered. She says her bees never forget the way to a flower, and that is why her clearing has stayed bright.
Marigold shows them the way out of the forest and wraps a honeycomb in leaves for the journey. She warns them that the Hushed have been seen near the forest edge, and that they must go carefully.
At the edge of the forest, the Hushed are waiting for them, and the grey figures close in from three sides. Soon the four friends stand in a ring of silent faces, with nowhere left to run.

Pell steps forward, opens the Long Memory, and begins to read out the names of the people of Millbrook. His voice shakes at first, but it grows steadier with every name, and the Dawnlight burns brighter.
At the name of Pip Cobb, a small boy in the front row blinks, and his hood slips from his head. Suddenly he looks around in confusion, and then he begins to cry.
Rook wraps her own blanket around the boy and leads him to the fire that Corin has hurriedly lit. Pip sobs for a long time, and then he tells them, in a small voice, that his name is Pip.
Pip says that being in the Grey was like standing in a room with no corners and no door. He remembers walking, and being very tired, and not knowing what it was that he had lost.
That night, Isaura and Pell talk quietly while the others sleep. Pell used to buy apples from Pip's mother, and he thinks that a name works best when it comes with a face and a story.
In the morning a kindly farmer named Hob Garrick comes along the road with a cart and a grey mare called Dumpling. When he hears the story, he offers to take Pip home to Millbrook at once.
Pip hugs Juniper and says goodbye to each of them in turn. He gives Corin a small blue marble, and tells him to keep it to remember a boy who got his name back.
They watch the cart roll away down the road until it is only a small dot. Corin feels happy for Pip, but he wonders how many more are still lost in the grey.
Isaura points her stick at the snowy mountains, which shine pink in the early light. “One person at a time,” she says, “and one mountain at a time.”

At the foot of the mountains the air is cold and thin, and the peaks seem to touch the clouds. Isaura looks up at Ironcrown, the highest of them, and says that her husband Tam once guided travellers there.

Isaura checks every pack and hands out thick boots, woollen hats and a long coil of rope. She teaches them to walk in snow with small, careful steps, and she makes them practise until she is satisfied.
Slowly the party climbs the Hightarn Pass, and soon the first snowflakes begin to fall. The path grows steeper and narrower, and the clouds sink lower until they hide the valley below.
On a high ledge Pell stops, white-faced, and tells them that he is terrified of heights. Corin takes his hand, talks quietly about the ferry, and walks him along the ledge one step at a time.
A deep crack in the ice blocks the path, and there is only a narrow bridge of frozen snow across it. Rook crosses first with a rope around her waist, and she laughs, which makes the others braver.
Isaura's knee has begun to hurt again, though she does not say so, and she walks closer to the lantern's warmth. Corin notices, and he quietly slows the pace without saying a word.
In the afternoon the wind rises, and the snow comes sideways in great white sheets. They tie themselves together with the rope and walk bent double, unable to see more than a few steps ahead.
Isaura spots a small stone hut beside the path, built long ago for shepherds. They stumble inside just in time, and Corin and Rook push the heavy door shut against the storm.

That night they huddle around the Dawnlight and share the last of their bread, while the storm howls outside. Each of them tells a story from home, about the river, the mountains, the library and the ferry.
Pell is the first to notice that the flame grows a little taller with every story. He writes it down in the Long Memory, and the others look at the golden light in wonder.
In the morning the storm has gone, and the world outside is white and perfectly quiet. Isaura goes out first to look at the path, and the others wait in the doorway.
Suddenly a grey mist creeps over the high ridge and rolls down the slope toward the hut. It moves faster than any mist should, and the snow turns dull and colourless where it passes.
Isaura steps in front of the others and plants her stick in the snow like a flag. She shouts at them to hold the lantern high, and then she turns to face the mist alone.
The Grey rolls over her, and for a moment she disappears completely. When it passes, she is still standing, but her shoulders have dropped and her face has gone strangely smooth.
Isaura turns and looks at them with a friendly, puzzled smile, and she asks them who they are. She has forgotten her name, her mountains and her friends, and she does not know why they look so sad.
Isaura tries to wander back down the path alone, humming softly to herself. Gently, Corin ties the rope around her waist, and she lets him do it, like a child.
Rook and Corin take an arm each and half carry her up the steep, snowy slope toward the top of the pass. Pell leads the way with the lantern, and he does not look back.
Pell is ashamed that he does not know how to help, and he turns the pages of the Long Memory as he walks. He reads and reads, and with every page his face grows more worried.
At last he stops, and he reads aloud an old note written by a Keeper long ago. It says that a name, spoken by someone who loves the person, may bring them back.
They find a shallow cave beneath the summit and light a fire in it. They sit around Isaura, who smiles at the flames, and they promise each other that they will not leave without her.
Rook says that if a name can bring Isaura back, they must tell her everything they know about her. They sit around the fire, and each of them tries to remember what she has said.
Rook speaks first, and she says Isaura's full name and her title in her kindest voice. Isaura only nods politely, as if she is being introduced to someone else.
Corin remembers the story that Isaura told in the stone hut, about the night she and Tam found a lost child on Ironcrown. He tells it slowly, and Isaura listens with her head on one side.
Pell closes his eyes and recites the same story word for word, exactly as Isaura told it. The Dawnlight burns brighter with every sentence, and the cave glows like the inside of a lamp.
Juniper pads across the cave and lays her chin on Isaura's knee. Isaura strokes the dog's ears without thinking, and she murmurs a name that sounds like Bramble.
Corin carries the lantern to the cave mouth and points to the great white peak that shines in the sunrise. “That is Ironcrown,” he says gently, “and you have walked every path on it.”
Isaura stares at the mountain for a long time, and then she whispers its name. Her voice cracks, and she says another name too, the name of Tam, and her eyes fill with tears.
Suddenly she turns, and the old gruffness comes back into her face. “I am Isaura Brack,” she says, “and my knee is complaining, and why is everyone staring at me?”
Later she tells them that being in the Grey was like falling asleep in a cold, empty room. Somewhere in that quiet, she says, she heard someone crying, very far away.
By midday they leave the cave and begin the long walk down the far side of the pass. Far below them, a vast white plain shines like a mirror in the sun.
Isaura leads the way down the stony path with strong, easy steps, as if she has never been ill. She tells them that the Salt Flats are a day's walk across, and that no one must stray from the road.
At the bottom of the mountain the Salt Road begins, marked by white posts that shine in the sun. The plain around them is so flat and bright that it looks like a huge mirror lying on the ground.
They walk all day with scarves over their faces, and the glare makes their eyes water. Strange pictures shimmer in the distance, and Isaura reminds them to follow the posts and nothing else.
That night they camp beside a great block of salt, under a sky so full of stars that it seems to continue under their feet. Corin lies awake and looks at the Dawnlight until at last he falls asleep.
In the middle of the night, Corin sits up and walks away from the camp without waking anyone. He does not remember getting up, and he does not notice that Juniper is following him.

Ahead of him, across the white ground, a village is shimmering, and it looks exactly like Saltreach. His mother stands in the doorway of the cottage, waving, and she looks so happy that his heart aches.
A soft voice in the air tells him that he has walked far enough, and that he can rest now. The lantern feels heavier with every step, and he thinks how easy it would be to put it down.
Juniper bites his sleeve and pulls with all her strength, and she will not let go. At the same moment, the Dawnlight flares in his hand, so brightly that he has to close his eyes.
When he opens them, the village has dissolved into white salt and a thin grey mist. There is no cottage and no mother, and he stands alone far from the road, with the cold wind in his face.
The others find him, and Rook wraps her cloak around his shoulders while he shakes. “The Grey does not tell lies,” she says quietly, “it only offers you the thing you want most.”
At the far edge of the plain the ground turns to sand, and the air begins to smell of salt and seaweed. Gulls cry overhead, and then Corin sees the sea for the first time in his life.
Port Larrow is a grey harbour town built around a curved stone quay, with a tall lighthouse above it. The lighthouse is dark, and there are no lights anywhere in the streets.
Fishing boats lie tied up in rows, and heaps of nets are rotting on the quay. Sailors wander slowly along the water's edge with nowhere to go, and nobody is feeding the gulls.
Isaura points up at the lighthouse and tells them that it once guided ships all along the coast. It stands on the hill where the Larrowhead Beacon burned, and now its lamp is cold.
A young woman with a sailmaker's needle in her hand comes running down the street toward them. She introduces herself as Tilda Vane, and she asks them to help her light the lighthouse again.
Tilda leads them up the spiral stair inside the tower, past a tall man who sits silent at its foot. He is her father, Osric, who kept the lamp for twenty years, and the Grey has taken him.
At the top of the tower the great lamp stands cold and silent in its glass room. Corin raises the Dawnlight and touches its flame to the wick, and the lamp bursts into golden life.
A beam of golden light sweeps across the harbour, across the dark water and out to sea. Wherever it passes, the Grey draws back, and the town shows clear and bright under the stars.
People pour out of their houses to cheer, and the sailors on the quay stop and lift their faces to the light. Some of them start to call out the names of their boats, as though from a dream.
That night they sleep at the Fisher's Rest, an old harbour inn, and Tilda brings them hot fish stew. Corin cannot sleep, because he knows that a single lamp can hold the fog back for only one night.

In the morning the grey mist is back at the edges of the town, moving between the last houses. The lighthouse lamp still burns, but its beam looks thin in the daylight, and Tilda says that her oil will not last long.
Late that afternoon, a silent sailor on the quay turns toward Corin and speaks, but the voice is not his own. It is deep and gentle and very tired, and everyone on the quay stops to listen.

The voice greets Corin by name, politely, as one greets an old friend, and it tells him he has done well. It asks him to give up the Dawnlight and rest, and it promises that nobody will be hurt again.
Corin's friends stand close behind him, and Rook reaches for her boat hook, but he shakes his head. “I do not want to hurt you,” he says, “and I will not give you the light, but I am listening.”

The voice is silent for a long time, and then it says, almost sadly, that Corin may come to Cairnhead if he dares. When it is gone, the sailor falls to his knees and looks around, as empty and confused as before.
They cannot go on by land, because the Grey is thick on every road to the north. Rook walks along the quay, studying the boats, and she looks pale as she does it.
At the end of the quay she finds a small sailing boat with a patched grey sail, called the Heron. Tilda says it belonged to her grandfather, and she insists that they take it.
The sail has a long tear in it, so Corin takes out his mother's needle and the coil of strong cord. He sews all afternoon, and Rook says that nobody has ever mended a sail so neatly.

The people of Port Larrow bring gifts for the journey: bread, cheese, barrels of fresh water and spare rope. The landlady of the Fisher's Rest gives them a large pot of stew and a warm blanket for each of them.
At dusk they push the Heron away from the quay, and Tilda waves from the lighthouse door. Behind them the beam of the lamp sweeps over the water, and ahead lies the open sea.
