For the first night the Heron sails smoothly under a clear sky, and Rook sings as she steers. Isaura, however, turns green and holds the rail, and she says that mountains are much more polite than waves.

The next day is bright and windy, and porpoises leap out of the water beside the boat. Rook laughs more freely than Corin has ever heard, and she says that she had forgotten how much she loved the sea.
That night Pell and Corin sit at the bow, wrapped in blankets, and watch the stars come out. Pell tells Corin the name of every star, and Corin says that he would be lost without him.
On the third morning a long grey fog bank lies across the sea ahead of them, as thick as a wall. Rook says that this is no natural fog, because it does not move with the wind.
By afternoon the Heron has sailed into the fog, and a storm breaks over the boat. Waves rise higher than the mast, and rain beats against the grey sail like thrown gravel.
Rook calls for the compass, and Corin pulls it out of his coat with cold, shaking hands. The needle spins round and round, and it points nowhere, because the Grey has confused it.
Corin notices that the Dawnlight is leaning in his hand, and he holds it up in front of him. “It knows the way,” he shouts over the wind, and he turns the boat to follow the flame.
Waves wash across the deck, and Juniper wedges herself under a seat with her claws out. Isaura ties them all to the mast with rope, and she says that this is almost as bad as the mountain.
Rook takes the helm beside Corin, and together they hold the boat steady against the storm. “I swore I would never go to sea again,” she shouts, “and look at me now!”
At dawn the wind drops, and the fog thins to a few grey ribbons. Through the last of the mist, they see a tall cliff ahead of them, with the dark shape of a ruined tower on its top.

The Heron slides into a small rocky cove at the foot of the cliff, and its keel grinds on the pebbles. Rook jumps out first and ties the rope to a rock, and then she sits down on the beach and laughs.
They rest on the pebbles and look up at Cairnhead, where the ruined tower stands against the clouds. Isaura says that it looks a very long way up, and nobody can argue with her.
At the back of the cove Isaura finds a stone stair cut into the face of the cliff. Small niches have been carved into the wall at every turn, and each one once held a lamp.
They begin to climb the narrow stair, with the sea booming far below them and the wind pulling at their coats. Corin goes first with the lantern, and Juniper stays so close that she trips him twice.
Pell counts the steps aloud to keep his mind off the drop, but he loses count at about three hundred. He says that this has never happened to him before, and he starts again from the beginning.
Behind them, a bank of grey fog begins to creep up the stair, step by step. It makes no sound, but the air grows colder, and the little sea birds fly away.
Isaura's knee has begun to hurt, and she climbs more slowly with every flight. Rook ties a rope around them both and takes some of her weight, and Isaura grumbles but lets her.
Halfway up, they rest in a ruined stone watch-house that has lost its roof. On one wall someone has carved words long ago: “Keep the light, keep the name.”
Looking down from the doorway, they see dozens of grey figures climbing the stair in a long, silent line. The Hushed are following the light, as they always do, without hurry and without rest.
The Dawnlight burns brighter with every step, until Corin's hands glow gold in its light. At last the stair ends at a broken stone gate, and beyond it lies the top of the cliff.
The summit of Cairnhead is windswept and bare, with the broken walls of the old tower at its edge. In the middle stands a great stone bowl, black with soot and cold as iron: the first Beacon.
Beside the bowl, a tall figure stands waiting, and he is made entirely of drifting fog. Around his neck hangs a heavy chain of silver, the chain of a Keeper of the Beacons.
Behind the travellers, the Hushed come up the last steps and gather at the edge of the cliff in a silent crowd. They do not come near the figure of fog, as though even they are afraid of him.

The figure speaks politely, and his voice is the same gentle voice that came from the sailor at Port Larrow. He tells them that he is the Pale Regent now, but that long ago his name was Ansel Dray, and he was Keeper here.
Ansel tells them about the winter when his wife Lena and his daughter Wren fell ill, and nothing could be done. He lit the Beacon every night and hoped, but it could not save them, and they died.
After they were gone, Ansel stopped lighting the fire, because it hurt too much to look at it. The pain never left him, so he went down to meet the Grey and asked it to take the pain away.
He believes that the Grey is merciful, and that he is helping the world by spreading it. In the Grey, he says, nobody weeps, and nobody has to remember the worst day of their life.
Isaura steps forward and tells him that she heard someone weeping inside the Grey, a long way off. “It was you,” she says, “and I do not think you are as comfortable as you pretend.”
Ansel does not answer, but he turns to Corin and holds out his pale hand. He asks, very kindly, for the Dawnlight, and he says that he will keep it safe forever.
Corin shakes his head slowly, and he holds the lantern a little closer. He is not angry, and he says so, but he says that the light is not his to give.

Corin sets the Dawnlight on the stone floor, and his friends gather in a circle around it, with Juniper at their feet. “A name is not enough,” Isaura says quietly, “so we must give it a face and a story.”

Rook tells how her mother used to sing to her on the river when she was small, while the barge rocked in the dark. As she finishes, the Dawnlight grows brighter, and the shadows on the stones grow shorter.
Isaura tells them about Tam, and about the lamp they lit every night in the window of their hut for lost travellers. Her voice is rough, but the flame leaps up as though it is delighted.

Pell speaks next, and he tells them about the smell of the library and his teacher Orla Finch, who taught him to read. Then he names every reader who ever sat beside him, and the list goes on like a river.
Corin tells them about Aldous under the willow, about his mother mending nets, and about his father, Davin, and the ferry at dawn. Juniper barks once, loudly, as if she wants to add something.
The Pale Regent flinches, and the fog around his feet begins to thin and tremble. The Hushed at the cliff edge stir, and some of them lift their heads to listen.
Corin faces the Regent and says that remembering a sorrow is not the same as being broken by it. “Your pain is proof that you loved them,” he says, “and that is not something to wipe away.”
Then Corin takes a step forward and holds out the Dawnlight in both hands. He says that it is not a weapon, and that he is not offering it to be taken, but to be shared.
The flame shines on the Regent's face, and his eyes fill with tears. Slowly he says his own name, then the names of his wife Lena and his daughter Wren, and he remembers the sound of Lena's laugh.
The Regent kneels on the cold stone and weeps, and the fog falls away from him like a torn cloak. With shaking hands, he takes off his silver Keeper's chain and lays it at Corin's feet.
At sunrise, Corin carries the Dawnlight to the great stone bowl of the Beacon and lifts it high. His hands are steady, and Juniper sits beside him with her ears up.
He touches the flame to the old black wood, and the Beacon catches with a roar of golden fire. The heat washes over them, and the whole cliff glows like the inside of a furnace.
Far away, on the highest peak of the Hightarn, a small bright point of fire answers. Then another leaps up in the north, and another in the east, until all six of the others have lit.
Pell names them aloud as they appear: Hightarn, Longmere, Thornhill, Millhill, Larrowhead and Marshend. Isaura says that she has not seen the country look like that since she was a girl.
As the sun rises, the grey fog on the sea begins to melt. It thins and lifts like breath from a window, and the water below is blue for the first time in years.
On the cliff top, the Hushed lift their faces to the sunlight and blink, and one by one they speak their own names. They look at each other with wonder, and some of them are already crying for joy.
Ansel Dray rises from his knees and says that he will stay as Keeper of Cairnhead. He promises to light the Beacon every night, and to tell the story of the Grey to anyone who climbs the stair.
The friends say goodbye to Ansel and sail home along the coast, and the sea is blue and calm. At Port Larrow, Tilda runs along the quay, and her father Osric, awake at last, opens his arms.

At Millbrook, Pell returns to his library and Isaura goes home to her mountain, and the friends promise to meet again. Rook and Corin take the Kestrel up the Wendle, and at Saltreach his mother runs down the lane to meet him.

A few days later, Corin and his mother climb to the Tower of Aldermoor, and he hangs the Dawnlight in its high window. It is no longer the last lantern in the land, but the first of many, and that night Corin sleeps in peace.

Mist lay on the water like wool, and the only sounds were the dip of the pole and the faraway cry of the herons. He was fifteen years old, and he loved the crossing more than anything else in his small, quiet world.

Juniper, his brown dog, rode at the prow of the ferry as solemnly as a captain, and she had learned to know every passenger by smell alone. For the people she liked she wagged her tail in a slow, dignified sweep, and for anyone she distrusted she gave a low and thoughtful growl. Corin had learned long ago to trust her judgement of a stranger far more than he trusted his own.

In the evenings Corin walked home to the little cottage at the end of the lane, where his mother Mara sat mending the village's fishing nets by the last of the daylight. His father Davin had kept the ferry before him, until a winter fever took him when Corin was seven years old. The two of them rarely spoke of it, but the memory lived in the house like an old and gentle song.

The same faces waited on the wooden landing each day with their baskets and sacks, and old Tobias the fisherman was always the first among them, his nets slung over one shoulder. Corin was not a talkative boy, yet he had a way of listening that made people tell him everything. In a village as small as Saltreach, that was a quiet kind of treasure.

On market day a company of travelling traders rolled into Saltreach with dust on their boots and strange news in their mouths. They spoke in low voices of a grey fog that had been rolling across the eastern lands, and of towns where every door still stood open but no one remained who knew whose house it was. Most of the villagers laughed, as people do when they are frightened, but a few of them looked uneasily toward the horizon.

That evening, beside a fire of marsh peat, Granny Wenna told the children the oldest story in Aldermoor, the tale of the seven great Beacons that had once burned from the cliffs to the mountains. The children were delighted and called it a fairy tale, but Corin, sitting a little apart with Juniper's head on his knee, noticed that the old woman's voice shook when she reached the part about the lights going out. When the tale was finished she did not smile at all, but sat staring into the fire for a long time.

At sunset the marsh birds rose all together into the sky, a great wheeling cloud of wings, and then, one flock after another, they fell silent and dropped back among the reeds. Where the sky met the land, a long bank of grey had appeared that had not been there the day before, low and patient and perfectly still. Corin felt a cold finger run down his back, though the evening was warm.

By nightfall the whole village had gathered on the ferry landing to watch the grey wall as it crept steadily nearer across the marsh, swallowing the reed beds one by one. Someone began to ring the old bell, though no one could say what good it would do, and the sound went out over the water and did not come back. Corin held Juniper close against his legs and found that his hands were trembling.

That night Corin could not sleep, and he sat at the window with Juniper pressed against his side while the fog crept in among the cottages. It moved along the lane without a whisper, smoothing the edges from the fences and the doorsteps, and it was colder than any mist he had known. When he laid his hand against the glass, the pane was damp, and for a moment he could not remember whether he had been afraid.

By morning the fog had thinned to a pale veil, but old Tobias the fisherman stood in the lane in front of his own door and made no move to go in. He studied the house as though he had never seen it before, with a gentle, puzzled smile, and when Corin spoke his name, he only looked at him and shook his head. Tobias could not remember who he was, and with a shiver Corin understood that the Grey had come to Saltreach.

All morning the villagers crowded around Tobias in the lane, and Nan Pruitt, the healer, examined him with her gentle, practised hands. She found no fever, no wound and no sign of any sickness she knew, and her face grew troubled as she searched. When his grandchildren wept because their own grandfather did not know their names, Corin turned away, unable to watch.

Corin knelt before the old man and told him his name, slowly and clearly, as though he were teaching a child to read. Tobias only smiled at him with a courteous, faraway look, like a stranger on a crowded street. By noon three more people in the same lane had gone quiet and bewildered, and the village understood that the fog was not finished with them.

That evening the villagers crowded into the old hall and argued fiercely about whether to flee the marsh or to stand their ground. Mara rose at last and said in her steady voice that they must keep a lamp burning in every window, for a lit house was harder to forget. The lamps were lit, but in the thickening fog every flame burned small and pale, and many of the listeners noticed it with a sinking heart.

Long after midnight, Corin could bear the silence no longer, and he slipped out with Juniper to look at the ferry and check its ropes. The dog stopped at the edge of the landing and began to whine, with her ears pricked toward the blackness of the river. Corin followed her gaze, and he heard the soft, uneven sound of footsteps coming through the fog.

Out of the mist stumbled an old man in a torn grey cloak, leaning on a stick and breathing like someone who had run a long way. He begged Corin to take him across the river before the fog could catch him, and beneath his coat a faint golden light glowed. Juniper, who distrusted most strangers, pressed her nose into his hand as though she had known him for years.

Corin helped him onto the flat boards of the ferry and pushed off into the dark, and as the little boat slid away from the bank, the fog drew back around it in a ring. The old man leaned against the rail and told him that his name was Brother Aldous Wick, and that he had been walking for many days. His voice was thin and tired, but his eyes were bright and kind, and Corin found that he trusted him at once.

In the middle of the river, with the water black and silent on every side, Aldous slowly opened his cloak. Inside lay a small lantern of old brass, and its flame burned golden and steady, bright as a morning star, and utterly unlike any fire Corin had ever seen. “This,” whispered the old man, “is the Dawnlight, the very last lantern in all of Aldermoor.”

He told Corin that Aldermoor had once been lit by seven great Beacons, tall fires that burned on hills and cliffs and mountain passes, so that no traveller was ever lost in the dark. One by one the Beacons had gone out, and with every one that failed the Grey had crept a little farther across the land. Now only this single flame remained, and Aldous had kept it safe in the Tower of Aldermoor for forty years.

Aldous glanced at the river bank, where tall grey shapes were standing very still in the mist, and his hands began to shake. He warned Corin that the Grey hunted the Dawnlight, for it was the only flame in the world that would never go out by itself. Wherever the lantern went, he said, the Hushed would follow, silent and patient and never tired.

From inside his cloak the old man drew a worn map, which he unrolled on the deck and held down with the lantern. His finger came to rest on a tall cliff at the very edge of the coast, marked with the name Cairnhead. If the Dawnlight were carried there, he said, it could light the first and greatest Beacon, and the other six would answer.

They reached the far bank at last, and Aldous sank down against the trunk of an old willow, breathing in short, painful gasps. Corin took off his own coat and spread it over the old man's knees, and Juniper curled against his side to share what warmth she had. The golden lantern stood on the grass between them, and the fog hung back from its glow like a shy animal.

Between breaths, Aldous told him about the Tower of Aldermoor, a lonely stone tower on the hills two days' walk upriver, where he had served as Keeper for forty years. Every night of those years he had trimmed the Dawnlight and watched over it, until the Grey crept close enough to touch the tower door. Then he had taken the lantern and fled, for he understood that a light locked away in a tower would only be a light waiting to be forgotten.

He held out the lantern in both hands, and at once the flame leaned away from him and bent toward Corin, like a flower turning to the sun. Juniper's tail began to wag, slowly and solemnly, as though the dog had always known how this moment would end. Aldous looked at the flame and then at the boy, and he nodded as a man nods when a long question has been answered.

Corin stepped back and shook his head, and for a moment he could scarcely speak. He told the old man that he was only a ferryman's son, that he had never been farther than the next village, and that someone braver and cleverer ought to carry such a thing. His voice cracked on the last word, and he looked away across the dark water.

Aldous smiled and answered that a ferryman knew one thing which heroes too often forgot. A river is never crossed all at once, he said, but one push of the pole at a time, and the long road to Cairnhead would be crossed in just the same way. The light did not need a champion, only a friend who would not put it down.

At last Corin held out his hands, and Aldous laid the Dawnlight in them, and it felt warm and strangely light, like a sleeping bird. The old man gave him two rules, speaking slowly, as one who has carried them a long time. “Never leave it alone in the dark,” he said, “and never give it to anyone who only asks sweetly.”

Aldous leaned his head against the willow and closed his eyes, and a look of great peace spread over his weathered face. Corin sat beside him through the long hours of the night, with Juniper at his feet and the lantern in his lap, and did not move. Before the first light of morning, the old man had slipped into a deep sleep, and he did not wake.

At dawn Corin crossed the river and fetched Wilf Gorse the carpenter and a few of the villagers who still remembered their own names. Together they carried the old man up the slope and buried him beneath the willow where he had rested, with a flat grey stone to mark the place. Nobody spoke much, but each of them laid a hand on the stone before they left.

Back at the cottage, Corin set the Dawnlight on the kitchen table and told his mother everything, from the stranger at the landing to the map and the cliff called Cairnhead. Mara listened without a word, her needle still in her hand, while the golden light moved softly across her tired face. When he finished she looked at the lantern for a long time, as if she were listening to it.

At last she said, very quietly, that the fog would come to their door as it had come to Tobias's, and that no wall or window would keep it out. Someone had to carry the light to the sea, she said, and the lantern had already chosen. Corin opened his mouth to argue, and then he saw that she was holding back tears, and he closed it again.

Mara worked through the night without resting, folding bread, hard cheese, dried apples and thick woollen socks into an old leather bag. Corin watched her smooth each wrapping with her work-roughened hands, as though she could fold her worry in with the food. The cottage was very quiet, and the Dawnlight glowed on the table beside her like a patient guest.

Just before dawn she took her net-mending needle from its place by the window, together with a coil of strong cord, and pressed them into his hand. It was the most useful thing she owned, she told him, and she wished it to travel the world with him. Corin closed his fingers around the cold bone and found that he could not speak.

Word spread quickly through Saltreach, and by sunrise those who still remembered themselves had gathered in the lane with lamps, whispering among themselves. Wilf Gorse shook Corin's hand as though he were a grown man, Nan Pruitt pressed a little pot of healing salve into his pocket, and somebody rang the old bell once, softly. Even Tobias's grandchildren came, holding hands, though they did not quite understand what they were waving at.

At the cottage door Mara held her son tightly and kissed his forehead, and she managed to smile, and she did not weep until he had turned away. Behind them, at the end of the lane, the pale fog was gathering again, patient and silent, like a tide that knew it would return. Corin did not look at it, but kept his eyes on his mother's face until the very last moment.

Corin walked out of Saltreach with Juniper at his heels and the lantern swinging gently from his hand, and he did not trust himself to speak. The path ran beside the river he had crossed ten thousand times, and for the first time in his life it led somewhere he did not know. Soon the roofs of the village were small behind him, and the marsh lay wide and silent on every side.

Once only he looked back, and what he saw was the village sinking slowly into the fog, like a drawing washed out by rain. Then he turned his face to the road again and held the lantern a little higher, and the grey mist on the path drew back from the light as water draws back from a stone. It was the first time he had seen it work for him, and it made him feel braver than he had any right to feel.

That night he made camp under an old hawthorn tree, with the river murmuring somewhere in the dark, and he lay awake for a long while, listening. The Dawnlight burned beside him in its small ring of gold, and Juniper laid her chin on his arm, as warm and heavy as a promise. It was, he decided, a great deal easier to be brave when someone was breathing beside you in the dark.

By morning the path had come down to the water again, and a broad barge with a patched red sail was drifting slowly along with the current. At the tiller stood a woman in a bright red scarf, and when she saw the boy with the dog and the glowing lantern, she waved both her arms as if she had been waiting for him all week. Corin raised a hand in return, though he was unsure whether to feel glad or wary of such a cheerful stranger.

She introduced herself as Rook Tarn, captain, crew and cook of the barge Kestrel, and asked in a cheerful voice what a boy and a dog were doing alone on the Wendle path. When Corin admitted that he had no money, she threw back her head and laughed, and said that river people never charged one another for a ride. “Besides,” she added, “you look as though you have a story, and stories are the only cargo I cannot buy.”

Rook listened to the whole of his tale without once interrupting, and when he had finished she looked at the lantern for a long, thoughtful moment. Then she said that she had always wanted to see the Beacons lit, and that she could carry him as far as Millbrook in two days, if the wind stayed kind. A rope splashed, the red sail filled, and the Kestrel slipped away into the current with a boy and a dog sitting happily on her deck.

All that day the Grey followed the barge along the bank, keeping pace with it like a patient, hungry animal waiting for a door to open. Each time it drew close, the Dawnlight blazed a little brighter and pushed the fog back, as though a wall of gold had risen between the lantern and the dark. Corin, who had never been so important to anything in his life, watched it with wonder and unease.

Rook proved to be a patient teacher, and on the long, straight stretches of the river she let Corin take the tiller while she coiled ropes and sang. He learned quickly, for a ferryman already understood currents and sandbars, and by the afternoon the old barge answered his hand as readily as it answered hers. She declared that he was wasted on a ferry, which made him blush all the way to his ears.

After dark, with the Dawnlight standing between them on the deck like a small campfire, Rook leaned back against a coil of rope and began to tell the tale of the Beacons. Long ago, she said, the people of Aldermoor had been weary of losing their travellers and their fishing boats to the darkness, and so they decided to build a light that no night could hide. Her voice dropped to a murmur, and Corin found that he was holding his breath.

She counted the seven Beacons on her fingers, naming them in the order that the first Keepers had lit them: Cairnhead, Hightarn, Longmere, Thornhill, Millhill, Larrowhead and Marshend. Each one stood in its own valley, she explained, and a Keeper climbed up to light it every evening at sunset, so that the fires could be seen from one hill to the next. It was said that on festival nights a traveller could walk from the sea to the mountains and never once be in the dark.

Later, when the stars were out, Rook admitted that she had not always been a river woman, and that she had once crewed a seagoing ship. After a great storm one autumn she had come ashore and never gone back, for the river was kinder, and a bank was always within sight. She laughed as she said it, but Corin noticed that she kept her eyes on the dark water.

On the second afternoon they passed a riverside village where dozens of people stood in a long, silent row along the bank. None of them waved, none of them called out, and every one of them turned a pale face slowly to follow the barge as it went by. Rook said nothing, but her hand tightened on the tiller until her knuckles were white.

That night Rook dropped the anchor in the middle of the river, far from both banks, and declared that nobody was going to creep up on the Kestrel while she was in charge of it. The Hushed could walk to the water's edge, she reasoned, but a barge on deep water gave them nothing to follow but a light and a rumour. Even so, she took the first watch herself, and she did not look at all sleepy.

In the small hours Corin dreamed that Aldous was sitting under the willow tree, trying to tell him something that the wind kept carrying away. He woke with a start to find the flame of the Dawnlight shivering, and Juniper pressed hard against his side, whining softly. Rook was already beside him, holding the lantern steady with both hands, and slowly the flame grew calm.

At sunrise a bend in the river revealed the smoke of many chimneys rising straight into the pale morning, and beyond them a cluster of mill wheels turning in the current. Rook pointed with her chin and said that this was Millbrook, the biggest town on the Wendle and the best place in the world to buy rope. Corin, who had never seen more than a hundred houses together, stared at the roofs as they crowded closer.

By midmorning the Kestrel slid beneath a stone bridge and tied up at a bustling quay, where porters shouted and gulls squabbled over scraps of fish. Corin had never seen so many people in one place, yet he soon noticed that many of them moved slowly and absently, like sleepers who had been woken too early. It was plain that the Grey had already begun its quiet work in Millbrook.

Corin followed Rook into the heart of the market, where stalls overflowed with wool and apples and coils of rope, and the noise rose around him like a river in flood. For a boy from a quiet marsh village the crowd was dizzying, and he held the Dawnlight close beneath his coat so that no one would see it glow. Juniper pressed against his leg, quivering, and for once she did not stop to smell anything.

At one stall a baker stood staring at her own loaves, quite unable to remember what they cost, while her customers waited with patient, vacant faces. A little farther on the town crier read out the same notice three times in a row, in the same flat voice, as though he had forgotten that he had just spoken. Corin looked at Rook, and Rook looked away, and neither of them needed to say what they had seen.

Rook pointed to a line of white mountains standing very small and sharp on the far horizon, and she told Corin that no sailor could take him over them. She knew rivers and harbours well, she admitted, but she knew nothing at all about snow, and she had no wish to learn it by accident. What they needed, she said, was a guide who had walked the Hightarn Pass and lived to talk about it.

In a corner of the market, a tall, weathered woman with a walking stick was studying a map that had been pinned to the side of a stall. Rook nudged Corin and whispered that this was Dame Isaura Brack, who had guided travellers across the mountains for thirty years and had never lost a single one. The woman stood very straight, with a face like a cliff, and her grey eyes missed nothing at all.

Corin explained, as politely as he could, where he needed to go, and Dame Isaura listened with her arms folded and her mouth set in a hard line. Then she shook her head and said that she was retired, that her knee was ruined, and that she had no intention of freezing on a mountain to please a boy with a lantern. Her tone was gruff, but she kept glancing at the golden light under his coat.

Suddenly a thief in a dark hooded cloak darted out of the crowd and snatched at the lantern with both hands, and the people near them scattered with cries of alarm. Corin held on with all his strength, the brass cutting into his palms, and Juniper leapt at the man's ankle with a furious bark. For one long moment the whole market seemed to hold its breath, and not a single stallholder dared to raise a voice.

From nowhere a young man with ink-stained fingers swung a great leather book through the air and struck the thief squarely on the side of the head. The thief let go of the lantern at once and crashed to the cobbles, and the sound of the book was like the slamming of a heavy door. A ragged cheer went up from the crowd, and a few people even clapped.

The thief scrambled to his feet and fled between the stalls, with Dame Isaura's walking stick tripping him not once but twice as he went. Over his shoulder he shouted that a voice like grey smoke had promised him bread and a warm bed if he brought it the light. Then he was gone among the carts and the crowds, and Corin was left trembling with the lantern clutched safely against his chest.

The young man smoothed the cover of his book, a thick, battered volume with a brass clasp, and introduced himself as Pell Ainsley, a scribe of the Millbrook library. The book was called the Long Memory, he explained, and it was his own record of every story, song and name he had ever read or heard. He added, a little sadly, that he had never forgotten anything in his life, and that this was beginning to feel like a burden rather than a gift.

Pell asked, very humbly, whether he might come with them, for the Grey had already taken his teacher Orla Finch and half the readers of the library, and he could not bear to sit and watch it take the rest. Dame Isaura looked at him, and at Corin, and at the lantern, and then she let out a long sigh and said that she supposed she would have to go. She did not mention it, but she had noticed that the pain in her knee had quietly vanished.

Rook left the Kestrel in the care of her cousin Dunstan, who worked at the Millbrook dock and had promised to keep the old barge as clean as a church. She patted the rail one last time, rather gruffly, and then the four travellers and the dog turned their faces to the road. None of them looked back until the last of the town's chimney smoke had sunk beneath the hills.

Dame Isaura took command at once, in the manner of someone who had never in her life been disobeyed on a hillside, and announced the rules of the journey. They would walk slowly and rest often, she said, they would eat when she said so, and nobody was to complain of blisters before the third day. Rook muttered that this was worse than serving under a sea captain, but she shouldered her pack and fell into step.

Around the fire that night, Pell opened the Long Memory and wrote in a small, neat hand by the light of the Dawnlight, pausing now and then to chew the end of his pen. Juniper, who had decided within a day that he was a friend, fell asleep with her head on his boot and her paws twitching in some private dream. Corin watched them both and thought that it was strange how quickly four strangers had become a company.

The Long Road was old and perfectly straight, running across the plain like a line drawn with a ruler, and a worn grey stone marked every mile along its edge. Pell told them as they walked that the Beacon Keepers had built it in the days when the seven fires still burned, so that travellers might always find their way from one hill to the next. He said it with such love that Isaura, for once, did not tell him to save his breath.

They passed a farm where a farmer sat cross-legged in the middle of his ripe wheat, doing nothing at all, while the golden stalks bent in the breeze and the crows came to feast. Corin offered him half a loaf of bread, but the man only thanked him with a courteous nod and forgot to eat it. It was a small thing, and it troubled Corin more than a shout could have done.

On the third afternoon Juniper stopped suddenly in the road and began to growl, deep in her chest, and Corin turned to look back the way they had come. On a low hill a long way behind them stood a dozen figures in grey cloaks, perfectly still, with their hoods turned toward the travellers. They did not wave, they did not call out, and they did not move.

All day long the grey figures followed, never coming closer and never falling farther behind, as though they were pulled along by an invisible rope. Dame Isaura told them quietly that these were the Hushed, folk taken by the Grey, who now followed the Dawnlight as moths follow a candle without knowing why. Corin felt pity for them and fear of them in the same breath, and he could not tell which was stronger.

At dusk they reached a roadside inn called the Wheatsheaf, whose windows glowed with a warm yellow light, and the innkeeper, Bess Harker, was delighted to see them. She fed them hot soup and fresh bread and told them in a low voice that half her neighbours had forgotten how to speak, and the other half were afraid to. For the first time in days, Corin ate until he could not eat any more.

In the middle of the night Juniper woke Corin with a low growl, and he crept to the window and looked out through the curtain. Dozens of grey figures stood in a perfect circle around the inn, without a sound, without a movement, and every pale face was turned toward the room where the lantern lay. Corin woke the others with a hand over his own mouth, as though even a whisper might break something.

Bess led them down to the cellar in the dark, moved aside a barrel with surprising strength, and lifted a trapdoor that opened into the barley field behind the inn. One by one they crawled out into the cold night air, with the Dawnlight shielded beneath Corin's coat, and then they ran across the furrows until the inn was only a faint glimmer behind them. The Hushed stood on around the empty building, patient and silent, and none of them seemed to notice that their quarry had gone.

Beyond the barley fields the Long Road ran straight into Thornwood, an ancient forest where the trunks grew so close together that the daylight turned green and thin. Soon the road dwindled to a narrow track, and the track dwindled to a rumour, and the travellers walked in single file with the Dawnlight held high in front. Even Juniper kept very close to Corin's heels, and she glanced at every shadow as though it might move.

Thorny branches reached across the way and tugged at their coats like beggars, and the path vanished beneath a carpet of dead leaves that no foot had disturbed for years. After an hour of turning and doubling back, Dame Isaura planted her stick in the ground and admitted, through gritted teeth, that she did not know where they were. It was the first time that any of them had ever heard her admit to such a thing, and nobody dared to smile.

That night they camped in a hollow beneath a vast, twisted oak, though no stars showed through the roof of branches and the darkness felt almost solid. Strange creaks and whispers drifted through the trees, and Corin noticed with a pang of worry that the Dawnlight was burning lower than it had burned before. He did not tell the others, but he sat up with it until the dawn, with one hand cupped around the glass.

Pell opened the Long Memory and recited, from a forester's map he had read as a child, every bend of every stream and the name of every clearing in the wood. Unfortunately the trees had grown since the map was drawn, and the paths had shifted with them, and nothing he remembered matched anything that they could see. He closed the book with a look of such misery that Rook patted him on the shoulder.

At dawn Corin lifted the lantern, and he saw that the golden flame was leaning gently away from the way they had been walking, toward a dark gap between two ancient oaks. Isaura raised one eyebrow, but she said that when a traveller is lost she should take any sign that she is given and be grateful for it. They gathered their packs without another word and followed the little tongue of fire.

The thorns seemed to draw back on either side as the flame led them through the gap, and the tangled undergrowth opened into something that was almost a path. Somewhere above them a bird began to sing, then another, and the air lost its smell of damp earth and took on the sweetness of flowers. Corin realised that he was smiling, something he had not done for days, and he felt almost guilty about it.

After an hour the trees opened suddenly, and they stepped out into a sunlit clearing, where rows of old straw beehives stood among the wild flowers. Thousands of bees drifted through the warm air in lazy spirals, filling the glade with a deep and peaceful humming that seemed to loosen the knots in everybody's shoulders. Juniper sneezed twice, sat down, and refused to go any farther until she had been properly introduced.

A woman in a wide straw hat came out of a small thatched cottage, wiping her hands on her apron, and looked at the strangers without the slightest surprise. She introduced herself as Marigold Fenn, the beekeeper of Thornwood, and without being asked she gave each of them a wooden spoon heavy with golden honey. It was the sweetest thing Corin had ever tasted, and for a moment it made him homesick.

While they ate, Marigold told them quietly that the Grey fed on forgotten things, and that it hated nothing so much as being remembered. Her bees, she said, never forgot the way to a flower, and she believed that was why her little clearing had stayed bright when the rest of the forest had grown dim. Corin looked at the golden honey on his spoon and thought about all the things he must never forget.

When they had rested, Marigold showed them the way out of the wood, and she wrapped a honeycomb in leaves and pressed it into Pell's hands for the road. She warned them gravely that grey cloaked figures had been seen drifting toward the forest's edge, and that the Hushed always seemed to know where the light was going. Then she lifted her hand and the bees rose in a golden cloud, as if they were saying goodbye.

The Hushed were waiting for them at the edge of the forest, as though the wood itself had breathed them out, and the grey figures closed in from three sides without a sound. Within a minute the four friends stood in a ring of pale, silent faces, with the Dawnlight blazing in Corin's hands and nowhere left to run. Isaura raised her stick, but she did not strike, for there was no anger in those faces to answer.

Pell stepped forward, to everyone's astonishment, opened the Long Memory and began to read aloud the names of the people of Millbrook, one by one, in the clear voice of a scholar. His voice shook at first, but it steadied with every name, and the Dawnlight rose to meet it, brightening until the shadows of the Hushed stretched far across the grass. He read the bakers and the boatmen, the weavers and the watchmen, and the whole ring stood listening.

At the name of Pip Cobb a small boy in the front row blinked, and his hood slipped back from a tangle of fair hair, and a look of dawning bewilderment crept into his face. He turned in a slow circle, staring at the tall strangers, the glowing lantern and the dark trees, and then his chin began to tremble. The rest of the Hushed did not stir, and Corin thought that he had never seen anything so lonely as that one waking child.

Rook wrapped her own blanket around the boy's shoulders and led him to the fire that Corin had hurriedly lit among the roots of a great elm. Pip sobbed for a long time, in the way that children sob when they have been brave for too long, and nobody tried to stop him. At last he wiped his eyes and told them, in a small voice, that his name was Pip, and that he was nine years old.

When he could speak, Pip said that being in the Grey was like standing in a room with no corners and no door, where everything was soft and quiet and nothing mattered at all. He remembered walking and walking, and being very tired, and not knowing what it was that he had lost, only that it had been something important. Rook listened with her jaw tight, and Corin saw that she was holding the boy's hand.

That night, while the others slept, Isaura and Pell sat on either side of the dying fire and talked in low voices. Pell had often bought apples from Pip's mother outside the library, and he thought that a name worked best when it came with a face and a story, and was not merely a word on a list. Isaura nodded slowly and said that she would remember that when the mountains came.

In the morning a kindly farmer named Hob Garrick came jingling along the road with a hay cart and a broad grey mare called Dumpling, and he stopped as soon as he saw the boy. When he had heard the story, with his hat in his hands, he said that he would carry Pip home to Millbrook that very day, and he would take no payment but a tale. Pip, still pale but quite steady, climbed up beside him on the high wooden seat, and Dumpling set off at a comfortable walk.

Before he left, Pip hugged Juniper hard around the neck and then said goodbye to each of the travellers in turn, in a grave, small, careful voice. He pressed a little blue marble into Corin's palm and told him to keep it, so that somebody would remember a boy who had got his name back. Corin closed his fist around the cool glass and promised, with all the solemnity he could manage, that he would never forget.

They stood in the road and watched the cart roll away between the hedges until it was nothing but a small dot at the end of the long grey line. Corin was glad for Pip, so glad that his throat hurt, but he could not stop wondering how many more were still wandering lost inside the Grey. Nobody answered his silence, because there was no answer that was not also a sorrow.

Isaura pointed her stick at the line of snowy mountains that stood across the sky ahead, shining pink in the early light like the teeth of some enormous sleeping animal. “One person at a time,” she said gruffly, “and one mountain at a time, and we shall do both.” Then she shouldered her pack and led the way toward the Hightarn Pass without looking round.

At the foot of the mountains the air was cold and thin and very clean, and the great peaks stood against the sky like the walls of a vast, silent hall. Isaura gazed up at Ironcrown, the highest of them, and told the others that her husband Tam had once guided travellers up its flank when they were both young. She said it lightly, but she did not speak another word until they began to climb.

Before the ascent Isaura inspected every pack like a general, and then she handed out thick boots, woollen hats and a long coil of hemp rope that she had somehow found in Millbrook. She taught them to walk in snow with short, careful steps, to keep three points of contact with the rock, and never to look down while they were moving. Rook asked whether there was a rule about complaining, and Isaura replied that there was, and that it was a very long one.

Slowly the party climbed into the Hightarn Pass, and before long the first snowflakes came spinning out of the low grey clouds. The path grew steeper and narrower with every hour, and the clouds sank lower until they hid the valley behind them and left only the rock and the snow ahead. It was a strange feeling, Corin thought, to be climbing into a world that had no beginning and no end.

On a high ledge, with the mountainside falling away in a sheer drop beside him, Pell stopped dead, white-faced, and confessed in a whisper that he had always been terrified of heights. Corin took his hand without making a joke of it, talked quietly about the ferry and the slow green river, and walked him along the ledge one step at a time. When they reached the broad rock beyond, Pell sat down and laughed until the tears came.

A deep crack in the glacier barred the way, and the only crossing was a narrow bridge of frozen snow that looked too thin to bear a bird. Rook tied the rope around her waist, crossed first with her arms spread wide like a tightrope walker, and laughed aloud when she reached the far side, which made all the others braver. Juniper, who did not need to be braver, trotted over in four quick steps and shook herself on the other side.

Isaura's knee had begun to hurt again in the biting cold, though she gave no sign of it, and she took care to walk a little closer to the warmth of the lantern. Corin noticed, as he noticed most things, and without a word he slowed the pace of the whole party until she could keep it comfortably. She gave him a short, sharp nod, which from her was a great deal.

In the afternoon the wind rose with a long, hollow moan, and the snow came sideways in great white sheets that stung every inch of exposed skin. They tied themselves together with the rope and walked bent double against the gale, unable to see more than an arm's length ahead and shouting to one another to be heard. Corin held the lantern against his chest and felt it pulsing softly through his coat like a second heart.

At the very last moment, when even Isaura could no longer find the path, she spotted the dark shape of a small stone hut beside the track, built long ago for shepherds and forgotten by everyone but her. They stumbled inside with the storm at their backs, and Corin and Rook leaned together against the heavy wooden door until it shut. The silence that fell was so sudden and so complete that it seemed to ring in their ears like a struck bell.

That night they huddled around the Dawnlight and shared the last of their bread and Marigold's honey, while the storm howled outside like a hungry wolf. To pass the long hours, each of them told a story from home, Rook about the river, Isaura about the mountains, Pell about his library, and Corin about the ferry. It was the sort of night that none of them would ever forget, though they could not have said why.

Pell was the first to notice that with every tale the flame grew a little taller, as though the story itself were fuel, and the golden light crept farther up the stone walls. In his small, neat hand he wrote down exactly what he had seen, and then he underlined it twice. By the time the last story was told, the little hut was as bright as noon, and the storm outside seemed very far away.

When morning came the storm had blown itself out, and the world beyond the door was white and utterly still, as though it had been wiped clean overnight. Isaura went out first to read the sky and the path, her stick tapping on the crust, while the others waited in the doorway with the Dawnlight between them. The air was so clear and so cold that every breath felt like a swallow of iced water.

Without any warning a bank of grey mist crept over the high ridge ahead and began to roll down the slope toward the hut, moving far faster than any mountain mist should move. Wherever it touched, the snow lost its sparkle and turned dull and colourless, like a candle flame seen through a dirty window. Corin felt the Dawnlight go tight and hot in his hands, and Juniper began to bark.

Isaura, who was standing some paces ahead of the hut and well beyond the lantern's reach, understood in an instant what the mist meant. She did not run for the light, but planted her stick in the snow and spread her arms wide between the Grey and the hut, shouting that the others were to hold the lantern high and not to move. It was exactly what she would have done for any traveller on any mountain, and she did not stop to think.

The Grey rolled over her like a slow grey wave, and for a long moment she disappeared from sight altogether, and the three watchers cried out her name. When it had passed, she was still standing there with her stick in her hand, but her shoulders had dropped, and her face had gone strangely smooth and untroubled. The Dawnlight flared behind the others, as bright as a trumpet, but it had come a moment too late.

Isaura turned and looked at them with a friendly, puzzled smile, as one might look at pleasant strangers on a road, and politely asked them who they were. She had forgotten her name, her mountains and her friends, and she did not understand why the three of them were standing there with such stricken faces. Rook put her hand over her mouth, and Pell sat down heavily in the snow.

Isaura set off down the track alone, humming a tuneless little song, as if she had somewhere pleasant to be, and nobody could make her turn back by words alone. Gently, very gently, Corin tied the rope around her waist and made the other end fast to his own belt, and she let him do it, with the trusting patience of a child. It was the hardest thing he had ever done, to lead the strongest person he knew like a lamb.

Rook and Corin took an arm each and half carried her up the long white slope toward the top of the pass, while Pell went ahead with the lantern to lead the way. The Hightarn was no place to dawdle, for the weather could turn again in an hour, and they did not dare to stop for anything but breath. Isaura chatted to them cheerfully about the clouds, and every word was a small knife.

Pell was overwhelmed by shame that he, who had read so much, had no notion how to help, and as he walked he turned the pages of the Long Memory with trembling fingers. He read as he climbed, and read as he stumbled, hunting through a lifetime of reading for a single useful line, while his face grew more drawn with every leaf. Behind him Corin watched his back and could do nothing, which was the worst part of all.

At last Pell stopped dead in the snow, and the colour came back into his face, and he began to read aloud in a voice that broke with relief. It was an old note written by a Keeper of the Beacons long ago, which said that when the Grey took a person, a name spoken by someone who loved them might bring them back. The others stared at him, and then at one another, and hope came into the cold air like a bird.

They found a shallow cave just beneath the summit, sheltered from the wind, and Rook lit a small fire in it with the last of their dry wood. They sat in a half circle around Isaura, who smiled gently at the flames and hummed her tuneless song, and they promised each other that they would not leave without her. It was a plain, quiet promise, and every one of them knew it was the most important thing they had ever said.

Rook said that if a name could bring Isaura back, then they must give her every name and every memory they had of her, and not stop until she woke. They sat close around the fire, and each of them cast back over the days of the journey for anything the old guide had said or done. It was the first occasion on which any of them had tried to hold another person steadily in mind, as one holds a flame against the wind.

Rook spoke first, in her kindest voice, and she said Isaura's full name and her title and the names of the villages she had guided travellers to. Isaura nodded politely, with a small, puzzled smile, as though she were being introduced to somebody else entirely. Rook sat back with her jaw working, and Corin understood that a name alone was only a key without a door.

Corin remembered the story that Isaura had told in the stone hut on the night of the blizzard, about the winter she and Tam had found a shepherd's child lost in the snow on the slopes of Ironcrown. He told it slowly and plainly, and Isaura listened with her head on one side, her eyes following the words as though they were small lights moving in the dark. When he reached the part about their old sheepdog Bramble, who had barked the whole way down the mountain, her fingers began to twitch.

Pell closed his eyes and recited the same story word for word, in exactly the voice and rhythm that Isaura herself had used, even down to the pauses where she had cleared her throat. The Dawnlight burned higher with every sentence, until the cave glowed like the inside of a lamp and the shadows on the walls grew thin and gentle. It was the first time his terrible memory had ever felt like a gift, and he knew it.

Juniper padded across the cave, climbed half into Isaura's lap, and laid her chin on her knee with a sigh. Isaura stroked the dog's ears without seeming to know she was doing it, and a name slipped out of her mouth like a bubble rising from a deep pond, a name that sounded very much like Bramble. The three friends held their breath, and nobody dared to move or speak for fear of frightening that fragile, rising memory away.

Corin carried the lantern to the mouth of the cave and pointed out, across the white valleys, to the great peak that was flaring in the sunrise like a crown of iron and gold. “That is Ironcrown,” he said gently, “and you have walked every path on it, and Tam walked with you.” Isaura came slowly to stand beside him, leaning heavily on her stick, and for a long moment she did nothing but look.

She stared at the mountain for a long time, as the colour deepened on its slopes, and then she whispered its name, and her voice cracked in the middle. She said another name after it, the name of Tam, and then her whole face crumpled, and tears ran down her weathered cheeks, and she did not seem to notice them. Behind her, Rook and Pell clasped each other's hands tightly and did not say a single word, for fear of breaking the spell.

Suddenly she turned, and the old gruffness came back into her face like the sun coming out from behind a cloud. “I am Isaura Brack,” she said, in a voice that rang off the rocks, “and my knee is complaining, and why in the name of the mountain is everyone staring at me?” Then she was laughing and weeping at once, and the four of them were holding on to one another as if they were still tied together by the rope.

Later, over the last of the honey, she told them that being in the Grey was like falling asleep in a cold, empty room where nobody was ever going to come and wake you. Somewhere in the middle of that quiet, she said, she had heard someone weeping, very far away, and she had not known why it had made her so sad. Corin said nothing, but he turned the thought over carefully, as he did with all strange things.

By midday they left the cave and began the long walk down the far side of the pass, with Isaura striding in front as though she had never been away. Far below them, as the cloud shredded and blew apart, a vast white plain lay shining in the sun like a mirror dropped from the sky. Pell stopped to stare, and the Long Memory gave him a name for it that he whispered with a kind of dread: the Salt Flats.

Isaura led the way down the stony path with long, easy strides, looking ten years younger than she had in the market, and she lectured them cheerfully about the plain below. The Salt Flats, she said, were a day's hard walking from edge to edge, and nobody who wandered from the marked road had ever been found by anything but luck. She spoke with such relish that it was clear she was glad to have her voice back.

At the foot of the mountain the Salt Road began, marked by a row of white posts that shone in the sun like the bones of some long-dead creature. The plain on every side was so flat and so bright that it looked like an enormous mirror laid on the ground, and the sky lay upside down in it, with its clouds and its birds. Corin had never seen so much light in one place, and it made his head swim.

They walked all day with scarves wrapped over their faces, and the glare was so fierce that their eyes streamed and the salt crust crunched like frozen snow beneath their boots. Strange shapes shimmered in the distance, towers and trees and ships that were not there, and each time one appeared Isaura repeated her one rule in a voice like a closing door: follow the posts, and nothing else. Even Rook, who disliked rules of every kind and had broken most of them on principle, said nothing against this one.

That night they camped beside a great block of rock salt, under a sky so crowded with stars that it seemed to continue beneath their feet, so that they felt they were lying on the roof of the world. The others were soon asleep, but Corin lay awake for a long time, watching the golden glow of the Dawnlight and listening to the great silence of the plain. At last, without knowing that it was happening, he too slipped away into a sleep that was deeper and stranger than any he had known.

In the middle of the night Corin sat up and walked quietly out of the camp, without waking a single one of the sleepers, and without any memory of having decided to do so. His eyes were open, but they were not seeing the plain, and he carried the Dawnlight in front of him like a man carrying a candle through a dream. Juniper woke at once and slipped out after him, her ears flat against her head, whining under her breath as she went.

Ahead of him, across the glittering white ground, a village shimmered in the moonlight, and it was Saltreach, every roof and every chimney and the crooked top of the old bell tower. His mother stood in the doorway of the cottage with a lamp in her hand, waving to him as she had so often waved from the landing, and she looked so happy that his heart ached. He began to walk faster across the glittering salt, and then, with the lantern swinging wildly in his hand, he began to run.

A soft, kind voice in the air told him that he had walked far enough, and that he had carried his burden for long enough, and that the time had come to rest. The lantern grew heavier with every step, until it seemed made of lead, and he thought how simple it would be to set it down at the cottage door and sleep for a hundred years. It did not seem like a danger at all, only like the end of a very long day.

Juniper caught his sleeve in her teeth and pulled with all her strength, planting her paws in the salt and growling through the cloth, and she would not let go however he tugged. At the same instant the Dawnlight flared in his hand, so brightly that it was like a sudden blow, and he flinched and closed his eyes. In that white blaze he felt the soft voice break, like a cord that has been cut.

When he opened his eyes, the village had melted away into white salt and a thin, grey mist, and there was no cottage, no lamp and no mother standing in the doorway. He was alone on the vast plain, far from the posts and the road, with the cold wind in his face and an ache in his chest that was worse than any wound. Juniper pressed against his legs, panting, and he knelt and hid his face in her fur.

The others found him there at last, following the glow of the lantern, and Rook wrapped her cloak around his shoulders while he shook. “The Grey does not lie,” she said quietly, sitting down beside him on the salt, “it only offers you the thing that you want most in the world, and asks very little in return.” Isaura said nothing, but she took his hand in her hard old fingers, and she did not let go until morning.

At the far edge of the plain the salt crust gave way to pale sand and low dunes, and the air began to smell of seaweed and wet stone. Gulls wheeled and cried overhead, and then, from the top of a dune, Corin saw the sea for the first time in his life, a vast grey-green plain that moved. He stood staring at it with the lantern dangling from his hand, quite forgetting to be tired.

Port Larrow was a grey harbour town built around a great curve of stone quay, and above it, on a hill of black rock, stood a tall lighthouse that had not been lit for a very long time. Not a window glowed in the crooked streets, and the whole town had the stillness of a held breath. Corin felt, with a small shock, that it was the first place he had ever seen which looked truly abandoned.

Fishing boats lay tied up in crowded rows with their sails furled, and heaps of nets rotted on the stones of the quay, with nobody to mend them. Sailors in salt-stained jackets wandered slowly along the water's edge, turning back at the end of the pier and walking the same way again, like the figures on a clock. Not a single child was feeding the gulls, and the gulls, offended, screamed at everyone.

Isaura stopped in the middle of the quay and pointed her stick up at the lighthouse, telling them that it had once guided ships safely along the whole coast, for a hundred miles in either direction. It stood on the hill where the Larrowhead Beacon had burned in the days of the seven fires, and now its great lamp was cold and dead. She spoke softly, and there was a sorrow in her voice that Corin had not heard before.

A young woman with a sailmaker's needle still pinned to her sleeve came running down the cobbled street toward them, out of breath and plainly astonished that anyone was moving at all. She introduced herself as Tilda Vane, and between gasps she begged them to help her light the lighthouse again, for she had seen the golden glow in Corin's coat from her window. Her eyes were red from weeping, but her chin was firm, and it was plain that she meant to be obeyed.

Tilda led them up the spiral stair inside the tower, passing at its foot a tall, silent man who sat on the bottom step with his hands on his knees, gazing at nothing. He was her father, Osric Vane, she told them quietly, who had kept the lamp for twenty years and had been taken by the Grey a month ago. She did not look at him as she spoke, and Corin understood that it was the only way she could.

At the top of the tower the great lamp stood cold and silent in its glass room, and the dust of many weeks lay thick on the brass. Corin lifted the Dawnlight, and his hand trembled as he touched its small flame to the wick, and for a long moment nothing happened at all. Then the lamp caught, and the whole room burst into golden life, as if somebody had opened a door in the sun.

A great beam of golden light swept out across the harbour, over the dark water and far out to sea, turning slowly like the hand of an enormous clock. Wherever it passed, the Grey drew back in long, trailing rags, and the town stood out clear and bright beneath the stars, every roof and mast and mooring ring. Tilda laughed and wept at once, and then she kissed Corin on both cheeks, to his great embarrassment.

People came pouring out of their houses to cheer, those who still remembered how, and the sailors on the quay stopped in their endless walking and lifted their faces to the light. Some of them began, haltingly, to call out the names of their boats, as though talking in a dream, and the sound went rippling along the harbour like the first birdsong of morning. At the foot of the tower Osric Vane turned his head to follow the beam, and he did not turn it back.

That night they slept at the Fisher's Rest, an old harbour inn whose landlady, a friend of Tilda's, brought them steaming bowls of fish stew and refused to take a penny. Corin lay awake in a bed that smelled of lavender and listened to the sea, knowing in his bones that a single lamp could hold the fog back for only one night. In the morning, the whole town would still be waiting for what he would do next.

In the morning the grey mist had returned to the edges of the town, moving between the last houses with the patience of a cat. The lighthouse lamp still burned, but its beam looked thin and pale against the daylight, and Tilda confessed, twisting her hands in her apron, that she had only a little oil left. Everyone in Port Larrow seemed to be looking at Corin, though nobody said a word.

Late that afternoon a silent sailor standing at the end of the quay turned slowly toward Corin and spoke, but the voice that came out of him was not his own. It was a deep, gentle, weary voice, like that of a man who has not slept for years, and everyone on the quay fell still to listen. The gulls themselves stopped crying, and the whole harbour seemed to hold its breath.

The voice greeted Corin by name, courteously, as one greets an old friend, and told him that he had come a long way and had done very well. It asked him to put down the Dawnlight and rest, and it promised, with every appearance of sincerity, that nobody in Aldermoor would ever be hurt or frightened again. It was the most dangerous thing Corin had heard in his life, because it sounded so much like kindness.

Corin's friends closed ranks behind him, and Rook reached for the boat hook she had been carrying, but he shook his head to stop her. “I do not want to hurt you,” he said, in a voice that was steadier than he had expected, “and I will not give you the light, but I am listening.” For a moment the sailor's pale eyes searched his face, and something in them flickered.

The voice was silent for a long time, and when it spoke again, it said almost sadly that Corin might come to Cairnhead if he dared, and that it would be waiting there at the top of the stair. Then it was gone, and the sailor fell to his knees on the stones, looking around him as empty and bewildered as before. Corin knelt beside him and helped him up, and he realised that his own hands were shaking.

They could not go on by land, for the Grey lay thick on every road to the north, and the coast path vanished into a bank of fog that no lamp could cross in a single night. Rook walked slowly along the edge of the quay, studying the moored boats one by one, and Corin noticed that her face was pale and her mouth was tight. She had said once that she had left the sea for good, and now the sea was the only way.

At the very end of the quay she found a small sailing boat with a patched grey sail and a name painted on her bow in faded blue letters: the Heron. Tilda said that she had belonged to her grandfather, who had sailed her up and down the coast for fifty years, and she would not hear of any payment. Rook put her hand on the old wood, closed her eyes for a moment, and nodded.

The grey sail had a long tear down one side, so Corin took out his mother's needle and the coil of strong cord and set to work on the quay, with Juniper guarding the spare thread. He sewed all afternoon with the slow, careful stitches of a boy who had mended nets since he could walk, and when he had finished, the seam was as strong as the rest of the cloth. Rook ran her thumb along it and said that she had never seen a better piece of work.

The people of Port Larrow came down in twos and threes to bring gifts for the voyage, bread and hard cheese, barrels of fresh water, a spare coil of rope and a brass compass that had belonged to a captain. The landlady of the Fisher's Rest carried down a great pot of stew with a lid tied on, and a warm blanket for each of them, and she cried as she handed them over. Corin was surprised to find that he was crying too, for he had never imagined that strangers could be so generous.

At dusk they pushed the Heron away from the quay, with Tilda waving from the lighthouse door and the whole harbour crowded on the stones to watch them go. Behind them the beam of the great lamp swept slowly across the water, gilding the waves one after another, and ahead lay the open sea, dark and enormous and utterly unknown. Rook took the tiller in a hand that was not quite steady, and with the other she raised the grey sail.

On the first night the Heron sailed smoothly under a clear sky, with the grey sail full of wind and Rook singing an old river song as she steered. Isaura, however, had turned an interesting shade of green, and she held the rail with both hands and declared that mountains were a great deal more polite than waves. Pell, who was perfectly well, offered her a piece of ginger, and she accepted it with the dignity of a queen.

The next day broke bright and windy, and a school of porpoises leapt and tumbled in the water beside the boat as if they had come to escort it. Rook laughed more freely than Corin had ever heard her laugh, and she confessed that she had forgotten how much she loved the sea, and how much she had been missing it. Juniper, sitting in the bow with her ears blowing back, wore the expression of a dog who had found paradise.

That night Pell and Corin sat together at the bow, wrapped in blankets, and watched the stars come out over the water one by one, brighter than any they had seen. Pell told Corin the name of every constellation and the story of how it had been named, until Corin said that he would be lost without a friend who knew so much. Pell said nothing, but even in the dark Corin could tell that he was smiling.

On the third morning a long grey fog bank lay across the sea ahead of them, as thick and tall as a castle wall, and it did not move with the wind. Rook watched it for a while with narrowed eyes, then said flatly that no natural fog ever stood still like that, and that it was waiting for them. Nobody disagreed with her, and nobody suggested turning back, though every one of them privately wished that somebody would.

By the afternoon the Heron had sailed into the fog, and a storm broke over the little boat with a violence that took their breath away, as though the sea itself had been waiting. The waves rose higher than the mast, the rain beat against the grey sail like thrown gravel, and the lantern's glow was the only colour left in the world. Corin gripped the rail with both hands and prayed that his mother's careful stitches would hold against the weight of the wind.

Rook shouted for the compass, and Corin pulled it out of his coat with hands that were numb and shaking, and held it up where she could see it. The needle spun round and round without ever settling, pointing in every direction and none, for the Grey had confused it as it confuses the minds of men. Rook swore once, softly, and then she fell silent, which Corin found a great deal more frightening than any shouting.

Then Corin noticed that the Dawnlight was leaning in his hand, quite steadily, as it had leaned toward the gap in Thornwood, and he lifted it high in front of him against the rain. “It knows the way,” he shouted over the howl of the wind, and he turned the boat's head to follow the little golden flame. For the first time since leaving harbour, the Heron seemed to be going somewhere.

Great waves washed across the deck, and Juniper wedged herself under a seat with her claws out and her eyes shut, refusing to be moved. Isaura lashed them all to the mast with lengths of rope, in the efficient way of a woman who had once tied a hundred travellers together on a glacier, and observed that this was nearly as bad as the mountain. Pell, soaked to the skin, held the Long Memory under his coat and said that he was perfectly all right.

Rook took the helm beside Corin, and the two of them held the boat steady together against the wind, shoulder to shoulder, while the sea heaved and boiled around them. “I swore I would never go to sea again,” she shouted in his ear, with rain streaming down her face, “and look at me now!” She was laughing, wildly and happily, and Corin realised with astonishment that she was no longer afraid of anything at all.

Toward dawn the wind dropped, and the fog thinned to a few grey ribbons that trailed away over the water like smoke from a fire that had gone out. Through the last of the mist they saw a tall cliff rising ahead of them, black and sheer against the paling sky, and on its crown the dark shape of a ruined tower. Nobody needed to be told that they had come at last to Cairnhead, where the first and greatest of the Beacons had stood.

The Heron slid into a small rocky cove at the foot of the cliff, and her keel ground softly on the pebbles, and the sound was the sweetest music they had heard in days. Rook leapt out first and made the rope fast to a boulder, and then she sat down on the beach with her face in her hands and laughed until the gulls complained. Corin understood that she was laughing because the sea had not beaten her, and he laughed with her.

They rested on the stones for an hour, with their wet clothes steaming in the pale sunshine, and looked up at Cairnhead, where the ruined tower stood against the clouds like a broken tooth. Gulls wheeled around its walls, crying, and the cliff itself seemed to lean over them as though it were listening. Isaura observed that it was a very long way up, and nobody could find a way of arguing with her.

At the back of the cove, half hidden by sea-grass and fallen rock, Isaura found a stone stair cut into the face of the cliff, worn into hollows by the feet of a thousand years of pilgrims. At every turn small niches had been carved into the wall, and Pell explained, running his fingers over them, that each one had once held a lamp, so that the climb to the Beacon was always lit. They were all empty now, and dark with age, and Corin thought that they looked like the eye sockets of something very old and patient.

They began to climb the narrow stair, with the sea booming on the rocks far below them and the wind tugging at their coats as if it wished to throw them off. Corin went first with the lantern held out before him, and Juniper stayed so close behind that she tripped him twice, though he did not have the heart to scold her. The steps were slick with salt spray, and every one of them kept their eyes on the stone in front of them and nobody looked down.

To keep his mind off the drop, Pell counted the steps aloud in a low, steady voice, and all went well until he reached about three hundred, when he lost his place entirely. He said that this had never happened to him before in his life, and that it was clearly the fault of the wind, and he began again from the beginning with great dignity. Rook said that it was the most reassuring thing she had heard in weeks.

Behind them, far down the stair, a bank of grey fog had begun to climb the cliff, step by patient step, as a flood climbs the rungs of a ladder. It made no sound at all, but the air grew colder as it came, and the little sea birds that nested in the crevices rose in a whirling cloud and fled out over the water. Corin quickened his pace without a word of warning, and the others, who had seen the fog as well, followed him at once.

Isaura's knee had begun to complain again, and she climbed a little more slowly with every flight, though she bit her lip and said nothing about it. Rook, without comment, knotted a rope around her own waist and Isaura's and took half the old woman's weight on her shoulder as if it were nothing. Isaura muttered that she needed no help, and then she accepted it, which was the highest compliment she knew.

Halfway up, on a broad landing, they rested in a ruined stone watch-house that had lost its roof to the storms of many winters, and sat with their backs against the wall to catch their breath. On the wall above them someone had carved a line of words long ago, in tall plain letters that the weather had softened but not erased: “Keep the light, keep the name.” Pell read it twice aloud in a hushed voice, and then he took out his pen and copied it carefully into the Long Memory.

Looking down from the doorway, they saw dozens of grey figures climbing the stair below them in a long, silent line, one behind another, with their hoods drawn up and their pale hands trailing along the rock. The Hushed were following the light, as they had followed it across every road and sea, without hurry and without ever seeming to tire. Corin counted the pale shapes until he could count no more, and then he turned away from the doorway and said nothing about what he had seen.

As they climbed on, the Dawnlight blazed brighter with every step, until Corin's hands glowed gold and the stones ahead of him seemed to be made of honey, and he felt as though the lantern itself were pulling him upward. At last the stair ended at a broken stone gate, with a gap where an iron door had once hung, and beyond it lay the windy summit of Cairnhead. They stood together before it, breathing hard and leaning on one another, and for a long moment no one had the courage to speak.

The summit of Cairnhead was windswept and bare, with the broken walls of the old tower crumbling along its edge and the grey sea sprawling to the horizon on three sides. In the middle stood a great stone bowl, black with the soot of ancient fires and cold as iron, and Corin knew without being told that this was the first and greatest of the Beacons. It looked as lifeless as a tomb, and as though it had been waiting for a very long time.

Beside the bowl stood a tall figure waiting for them, and he was made entirely of drifting fog, so that the wind passed through him and the sea showed faintly through his chest. Around his neck, bright and strangely solid, hung a heavy chain of silver links, the chain that a Keeper of the Beacons wore on the night that he was sworn. He turned his pale, handsome, hollow face toward them, and he smiled as a host smiles at guests who have come a very long way.

Behind the travellers the Hushed came up the last steps one by one and gathered at the edge of the cliff in a silent crowd, their grey cloaks stirring in the wind. They did not come near the figure of fog, but kept a careful distance, as a congregation keeps back from an altar. Corin was glad that they had stopped, and yet he did not like the look of their waiting.

The figure spoke at last, courteously, and Corin knew his voice at once for the gentle and weary one that had come out of the sailor on the quay at Port Larrow.
