He said that the people of the Grey called him the Pale Regent now, but that long ago, before the lights went out, his name had been Ansel Dray, and he had been Keeper of this very Beacon. He bowed his head a little as he said it, like a man recalling an old joke.

Ansel told them, in his low, patient voice, about the winter when his wife Lena and his little daughter Wren had fallen ill with the sickness that came off the sea, and about the physicians who could do nothing. Night after night he had climbed the stair to light the great fire, hoping against all sense that its glow might heal them, but it had not saved them, and in the spring he had buried them both. The wind seemed to drop as he spoke, as if it too were listening.

After they were gone, he said, he had stopped lighting the fire, because it hurt too much to look at it, and then the other Keepers had grown careless, and one by one the Beacons had gone dark. The pain had never left him, however, so at last he had walked down to the edge of the sea, where the first grey mist was rolling in, and asked it to take that pain away. The mist, he added with a thin smile, had been only too glad to oblige, and it had taken a great deal more than he had asked.

He told them that he did not think of the Grey as a wickedness but as a mercy, a soft grey blanket for the whole weary world, and that he was only helping it to spread. In the Grey, he said, nobody wept, nobody grieved, and nobody had to remember the worst day of their life, and he could not see what was so terrible in giving people peace. His voice was full of such sincere sorrow that, for a moment, Corin almost agreed with him.

Isaura stepped forward, leaning on her stick, and studied the figure of fog for a long moment with her sharp grey eyes. “I heard someone weeping inside the Grey, far off in the quiet,” she said, “and it was you, and I do not think that you are nearly as comfortable as you pretend to be.” For the first time, the Pale Regent had no answer ready, and the fog around him seemed to shiver.

Ansel did not answer her, but he turned to Corin instead, and he held out his pale hand with the palm turned upward, in the manner of someone asking for a small and reasonable favour. He asked, very kindly, for the Dawnlight, and he promised that he would keep it safe forever, in a place where no harm could come to it or to anyone who had ever loved it. The offer hung in the cold air like a bell that has not yet been rung.

Corin shook his head slowly, and held the lantern a little closer against his chest, and he found that there was no anger in him at all, only a great and quiet sadness. He told the Regent, in a voice that shook but did not break, that the light was not his to give away, and that he had promised an old man under a willow tree. The Regent looked at him for a long time, and the fog around his feet began to curl and stir.

Corin knelt and set the Dawnlight down upon the stones, and his friends came and stood about it in a ring, with Juniper at their feet, facing the figure of fog. “A name is not enough,” Isaura said quietly, “so we must give it a face and a story, as Pell did in the forest, and we must tell the truth.” Nobody questioned her, and nobody was afraid, although every one of them was trembling a little.

Rook went first, and she told them how her mother used to sing to her on the river when she was small, while the barge rocked gently in the dark and the water talked against its sides. She did not sing it, for she said she had no voice, but she remembered every word of the song, and as she spoke them, the Dawnlight grew brighter. The shadows on the stones drew in around the ring like timid animals, and then, one by one, they lay down and went still.

Isaura told them about Tam, and about the lamp they had lit every night in the window of their hut on the mountainside for the sake of any traveller who might be lost, whether or not anyone ever came. Her voice was rough as bark, and it broke twice, but the flame leaped up as if it were delighted and flung her shadow, tall and straight, across the whole summit. She said afterwards that it was the first time she had told the story to anyone.

Pell spoke next, hesitantly at first, about the smell of the Millbrook library and his teacher Orla Finch, who had put the first book in his hands and called a mind a lamp that wanted filling. He recited the name of every reader who had ever sat beside him at the long oak tables, and the list went on and on, as quiet and as beautiful as a river. Even the Hushed lifted their heads to listen to it, and a few of them, to Corin's astonishment, were mouthing the names along with him.

Corin told them about Aldous asleep under the willow tree, about his mother mending nets by the lamp, and about his father Davin and the ferry at dawn with the herons crying. Juniper barked once, very loudly, as though she wished to add that she had been there for most of it and had a great deal to say on the subject. The flame leaped up in answer, and the whole summit blazed gold from the broken tower to the very edge of the cliff.

The Pale Regent flinched as though the light had struck him, and the fog around his feet began to thin and tremble, and long pale threads of it drifted away on the wind. At the edge of the cliff the Hushed stirred, their hoods turning, and some of them lifted their faces to the glow like sleepers moved by a dream. Ansel Dray said nothing at all, but his silver chain trembled against his chest.

Corin stepped forward and looked up into the hollow, handsome face and said, as gently as he could, that remembering a sorrow was not the same thing as being broken by it. “Your grief is only the shape of how much you loved them,” he said, “and a thing like that is not meant to be wiped away, but to be carried, with help.” He had not known that he knew such a thing until he heard himself say it.

Then he took another step and held out the Dawnlight to the Regent in both hands, with the flame leaning toward the fog like a child reaching up to be lifted. He told him that it was not a weapon, and that he was not offering it to be taken, but to be shared, as the stories had been shared. The silence that followed was so deep that Corin could hear the sea breaking far below.

The golden flame shone on the Regent's face, and his eyes, which had been empty as wells, suddenly filled with tears that seemed almost too bright to look at. Slowly, as a man who has woken from a long sleep, he said his own name aloud, and then the names of his wife Lena and his daughter Wren, and then he remembered the exact sound of Lena's laugh. It came back to him whole and unharmed, like a bird returning to a window, and the force of it broke him open.

Ansel Dray sank to his knees on the cold stone and wept, and the fog fell away from him in long grey rags, like a cloak that had been worn through. With shaking hands, he took off the silver Keeper's chain that he had worn for so many bitter years, and he laid it carefully at Corin's feet. It lay there in the lantern light, bright and small, as if it were relieved to be put down.

At sunrise Corin carried the Dawnlight to the great stone bowl of the Beacon and lifted it high in both hands, with the first rays of the sun just touching the sea. His hands were steady, though his heart was not, and Juniper sat close beside him with her ears pricked as if she understood what was about to happen. Behind him his friends stood in a line, and the Hushed waited silently on the cliff.

He touched the flame of the lantern to the old black wood that Ansel had laid there in the days when he still believed in the fire, and the Beacon caught with a roar of golden light. The heat washed over them like a wave, and sparks went spiralling up into the morning sky until the whole cliff glowed like the inside of a furnace. It was the first time in many years that Cairnhead had worn its crown.

Far away on the highest shoulder of the Hightarn, a small bright point of fire answered, as sudden as a struck match, and then another leapt up in the north, and another in the east. One by one, across the dark and waking land, the other Beacons woke, as if each one had been listening all this time for the sound of the first. Corin was crying, and he did not mind in the least who saw it, for the whole country seemed to be weeping and laughing with him.

Pell named them aloud as they appeared, Hightarn, Longmere, Thornhill, Millhill, Larrowhead and Marshend, and every name was a small, glad ring of a bell. Isaura said, in a voice that was not quite steady, that she had not seen the country look like that since she was a girl, and Rook put an arm round her without a word. The whole of Aldermoor was joined again by a chain of golden fire, from the sea to the mountains.

As the sun climbed the sky, the grey fog on the sea began to melt, thinning and shredding and lifting like breath from a window in the warmth of a room. The water below Cairnhead turned from slate to blue for the first time in years, and the first gulls came wheeling back across it with great cries of joy. It seemed to Corin that the whole world was taking a long, deep breath.

On the cliff top the Hushed lifted their faces to the sunlight and blinked, as people do who have been asleep for a very long time, and one by one they spoke their own names aloud. They turned to look at one another with wonder, and some began at once to ask about children and neighbours and houses, and many were laughing and weeping together. Rook said that it was a great deal like a market day, and that she had never been so glad of a crowd.

Ansel Dray rose slowly from his knees and said, in a clear and steady voice, that he would stay as Keeper of Cairnhead, and that he would light the Beacon every evening until the end of his days. He promised, too, that he would tell the true story of the Grey to anyone who climbed the stair, so that nobody should ever be tempted by its soft voice again. Then he thanked Corin, simply and warmly, and took his hand in both of his own, as a man takes the hand of an old and dear friend.

The friends said goodbye to Ansel on the windy summit and sailed home along the coast, over a sea as blue and calm as a bowl of milk, with the Heron's grey sail full of a kindly wind. At Port Larrow the lighthouse was burning in the daylight, and Tilda ran the whole length of the quay with her arms wide, for her father, awake at last, was standing at its end. Corin turned his face away to let them have their moment, and found that Rook was doing the same.

At Millbrook, Pell hurried back to his library and his teacher, and little Pip flung himself upon Corin with a shout, while Isaura set out for her mountain. Rook and Corin took the Kestrel up the green Wendle, and at Saltreach his mother Mara ran down the lane to meet him and held him as tightly as she had on the night he left. Old Tobias stood waiting at the landing with his grandchildren clustered around him, and he knew every one of their names.

A few days later Corin and his mother climbed the hill path to the Tower of Aldermoor, and he hung the Dawnlight in its high window, beside the Keeper's old empty chair. It was no longer the last lantern in the land, but the first of many, and from that window a traveller could see, far away to the east and the south, the golden points of other Beacons. That night, with Mara asleep in the old chair and Juniper at his feet, Corin sat watching the flame and for the first time in months felt entirely at peace.
